title: Iran-linked threat prompted U.S. to move bombers from U.K., Trump says
description:
US President Donald Trump said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from a British airbase. 
   The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran. Last week, five British ‌men were arrested near the base — which Iran's Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target — on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts. 
   "We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why ‌would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them," Trump told reporters on Monday.
fullText:
LONDON/WASHINGTON, Oct 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said on Monday that a threat linked to Iran had prompted the removal of American B-1 bombers from a British airbase.

The planes had been stationed at RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers, and had recently been used in US strikes on Iran. Last week, five British ‌men were arrested near the base — which Iran's Revolutionary Guards previously said was a legitimate target — on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts.

"We had an idea that there might be a threat, and why ‌would I leave them there? It costs very little money to move them," Trump told reporters on Monday. "So we had a threat, and if we're going to be threatened, we just move them, and that sort of alleviates that. And we actually know the people ​that made the threat."

When asked if they were linked to Iran, Trump responded: "They would be linked to Iran."

Earlier on Monday, Vice President JD Vance said the US moved the bombers out of an abundance of caution.

"We do feel with some confidence that the Iranians are, you know, they're trying to do what the Iranian state has done for 49 years, which is engaged in acts of terrorism against the United States (and others), so we are being extremely cautious, and that's all I'd say about that," Vance told reporters.

However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there was no direct link between the sudden removal of the bombers and the suspected Iranian plot. He said the Pentagon is "constantly reallocating resources where ‌they need to be."

A NATO military source had said on Monday: "It is still ⁠believed that Iran poses an acute threat to US assets in the UK."

While much about the incident remains unexplained, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said any plot was likely backed by Iran.

Iran has said accusations that it was involved in any plot are baseless, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi wrote on X: "I can confirm Iran's belief that releasing supposed ⁠terrorists working for foreign states really says it all. You're barking up the wrong tree."

Rubio said on Monday the US had confidence in the security of all its bases.

Fairford, located 90 miles (145 km) west of London, is one of the most important European bases for the US, being one of only a few suitable for heavy bombers such as the B-1 aircraft. It has played a key role in previous US campaigns in the Middle East, although its ​bombers ​are not stationed there permanently.

During the current conflict, the US had permission to use Fairford only to strike Iranian missile sites ​that were attacking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, or so-called defensive strikes. London had ‌refused permission for the US to use British bases for offensive strikes on Iran.

That approach has strained ties between the US and Britain, typically one of Washington's closest allies.

A Pentagon official confirmed on Sunday that all US bombers that had been deployed to Fairford had headed to their home stations in the US.

The Pentagon said the US bomber force remained ready to deliver precision global strike capabilities "anywhere, anytime".

The New York Times, citing two US officials, said the US had rushed over the weekend to move the bombers after commanders received new threats about an Iran-backed plot. It said some of the planes had left while aerial refuelling aircraft were still being scrambled.

A US official declined to comment. The British government also declined to comment, although a spokesman for Burnham said the base was safe.

Christoph Bergs, research analyst at defence think tank the Royal United Services Institute, said the redeployment would in the ‌short term reduce US capacity "to quickly surge sorties against Iran, reducing the threat level somewhat".

But he noted that use of Fairford ​was already limited given London's stipulation on defensive strikes. The aircraft could now potentially be sent to either Diego Garcia or bases in ​the Gulf, to reduce the need for more air-to-air refuelling to cover the additional distance, but ​that would depend on capacity availability, negotiations with allies and security, he added.

TRUMP SAID PLOT WAS FOR 'BIG DAMAGE'

In the early hours of September 27, five British men in their 20s ‌were arrested after being seen running into fields from three white vans parked near ​the base. Police said no explosive devices were found ​but a quantity of petrol was present.

The men have since been released on bail. A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national arrested on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts four days later, has also been released on bail.

Trump said at the time of the first arrests that the plot had planned "big damage" and that it might have been connected to Iran. Trump later said he would not have released the ​suspects on bail.

A senior NATO military official said the removal of the bombers would ‌have no impact on the alliance: "NATO's defensive agility towards any aggression remains unchanged and unmatched thanks to the unity, strength, and combined capabilities of 32 nations."

The Wall Street Journal first reported ​the removal of the US bombers.

title: Trump uses anti-trans slur against Democratic Senate candidate in South Carolina
description:
Democratic Senate candidate Annie Andrews speaks at the Spratt Issues Conference in Florence, S.C., on Aug. 22. (Sean Rayford / Getty)
President Donald Trump used an anti-trans slur Monday to attack the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina as he urged voters to back Republican Sen.
fullText:
President Donald Trump used an anti-trans slur Monday to attack the Democratic nominee for the Senate in South Carolina as he urged voters to back Republican Sen. Darline Graham.

In a Truth Social post, Trump referred to Democratic candidate Annie Andrews three times as “trannie.” He said Andrews, who is not transgender, is “not for South Carolina.”

“And South Carolina must show, in the upcoming Election, that it is not for her,” Trump added.

Andrews responded by largely ignoring the insult, saying in a statement first shared with NBC News that she will “work with anyone to put South Carolina first.”

“As a mom and a pediatrician, I’m in this race to fight for my patients, my three kids, and South Carolina,” Andrews said, adding that “lowering costs and making life better for families across our state is going to take all of us working together.”

“If you care more about your bills than the politics in Washington, this campaign is for you,” she said.

Graham’s campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the post by Trump, who often uses insulting nicknames for politicians and officials he dislikes.

Reached for comment on why Trump used the slur, the White House referred NBC News to his social media post.

The Human Rights Campaign, an LGBTQ advocacy organization, blasted Trump’s remarks, calling them “the sad, disgusting, pathetic diatribes of a lame duck president with record-low approvals.”

“So low, in fact, he’s having to campaign in deep red territory in a desperate attempt to shore up support ahead of the midterms,” Ramiro Sarmiento, a spokesperson for the organization, said in a statement.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., condemned Trump’s words Monday night, calling his attacks on Andrews “despicable.”

“Annie Andrews is a mom and pediatrician who’s always put her community first — and she’s exactly who South Carolina needs representing them in the Senate,” Schumer said on X.

Andrews, a physician, has previously said she does not support gender-affirming surgery for minors or transgender athletes’ participating in women’s sports.

Former South Carolina Gov. David Beasley, a Republican, criticized the president for his attack on Andrews, asking voters to “reject politics based on division and hate.”

“This is abhorrent. Elections don’t have to be about cruelty and lies. South Carolina deserves better,” Beasley wrote Monday night on X.

Graham is running to keep her seat after Gov. Henry McMaster appointed her to fill her late brother’s seat after Lindsey Graham died in July.

Graham won the Republican primary in a runoff against Rep. Ralph Norman by nearly 5 percentage points. She has leaned heavily on Trump’s endorsement to make her case to South Carolina.

While South Carolina has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly three decades, the nonpartisan Cook Political Report shifted its rating of the race toward Democrats last month, moving it from “Solid Republican” to “Likely Republican.”

title: Republicans pour $700 million into midterms as red states turn competitive
description:
President Donald Trump arrives to speak at Butler High School in Vandalia, Ohio, on Sunday. (Mark Schiefelbein / AP)
Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime Republican states and districts.
Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer.
By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month.
fullText:
Republicans are swamping House and Senate races with an unprecedented flood of late ad spending as the party tests whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy it some reprieve from the eroding political environment that’s threatening longtime Republican states and districts.

Since the start of September, Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races alone, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. That’s new money on top of what had already been committed to those races in ad reservations made over the summer.

The disparity is greatest in the battle for the Senate majority, where almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans. That’s led by a massive, late investment in the Senate race in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico is threatening a longtime Republican seat and the GOP has poured in almost $150 million in new ad dollars to back up its nominee, Ken Paxton.

The gap is smaller in the House, where a bit less than 6 in 10 of those new ad dollars are coming from the GOP.

Democrats still have a number of advantages in their corner, including President Donald Trump and his party’s eroding standing among voters, Democrats’ own well-funded candidates, and help from outside groups. Candidates can take advantage of a rule that allows them to buy television ads at cheaper rates than outside groups, too.

But the color of the outside money flood shows how Republicans, increasingly on defense in both the House and the Senate, are able to lean on their financial advantage in hope of defying political gravity, as party bastions like Texas and even Kansas look more competitive than usual.

“With the environment not on our side and an incumbent presidency, the three things we have going for us are good candidates, a good map and a lot more money than they do,” said a Republican strategist involved in Senate races.

Everything about the late flood of ad spending is bigger in Texas, where a new group called Texas PAC has booked more than $115 million over the last month alone aimed at boosting Paxton, the state attorney general. Democrats haven’t won a statewide election in Texas in more than 30 years.

But because Republicans are spending largely through outside groups, they have to pay a premium on the rates for each ad, while Talarico’s flush campaign is able to capitalize on those lower candidate ad rates. That means the spending disparity is greater than the actual number of ad airings or their reach.

Senate races in Ohio and Michigan also drew more than $75 million in new ad dollars in September, mostly from Republican-aligned groups. They include a super PAC funded by cryptocurrency interests, Trump’s aligned super PACs and other groups aligned with the national party or Senate Republican leadership.

Again, both states have Democratic candidates — former Sen. Sherrod Brown in Ohio and former county health official Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan — who have been spending significant money on their advertising campaigns.

No Going Back PAC and Safety and Affordability PAC have made more than $150 million in new ad bookings since the start of September across dozens of races. While the groups haven’t confirmed where they’ve gotten their war chest from, The New York Times recently confirmed that MAGA Inc., Trump’s main super PAC, is primarily funding the effort with the hundreds of millions of dollars it has banked over the last few years.

Sen. Tim Scott of South Carolina, chair of the Senate GOP’s campaign arm, touted the party’s spending advantage as key to helping Republicans hold on to their majority and credited Trump’s deep-pocketed political operation with ensuring the flood of cash continues.

Scott told reporters that he met last week with Trump’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles, and that the message from Wiles was “money will not be our problem.”

“That’s exciting news to me,” Scott said, adding later, “Knowing that they are going to invest completely in these races is incredibly helpful, because cash is king.”

“We finally find ourselves at a cash advantage because of MAGA Inc. It’s a powerful tool that is providing us with the firepower necessary to really share our message,” he said.

Democrats take some solace in where the new spending is going. The vast majority is plowing into states and seats Trump carried in 2024, including congressional districts Trump would have won by double digits that year, like North Carolina’s 1st District, Texas’ 35th District and Alaska’s at-large congressional district.

The money is also going to races in which Republicans felt comfortable until recently, like the Senate race in Kansas, where the top Senate Republican super PAC just reallocated millions initially meant to be spent in North Carolina.

“The money is not because there is this swell of Republican momentum; the money is because of a swell of Republican panic,” said Lauren French, the communications director at Senate Majority PAC, the super PAC aligned with Senate Democratic leadership. “Voters don’t like anything they are selling — that includes the message, the candidates and the president.”

Meredith Kelly, a longtime Democratic strategist who works on House and Senate races, said, “When you are defending in such deep-red territory, the technical term for that is: ‘You’re f---ed.’”

“Republicans, if they have one advantage, it’s that they have more money, and they are putting that money to the test right now post-Labor Day,” Kelly added. “However, the big question is: Is that money enough to counteract the fact that Donald Trump’s coalition is falling apart?”

Still, Democrats are uncomfortable watching their party get outspent to such a degree.

“It’s a huge problem, and it will be an ongoing problem, and you see all the lists of high-value donors for both parties and we get swamped every time,” Kelly said. “It creates such an initial advantage for the Republicans that we have to close the gap on in a variety of ways — candidate money, better message, better candidates. We are setting ourselves up for an uphill battle every single time because of the Republican donor strength in terms of the billionaire class.”

title: Russia says no plague cases detected among contacts of deceased lab worker
description:
Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among people who had come ‌into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died ‌last week. 
   Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in ​a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump. 
   Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 ‌days and that extensive testing ⁠had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work. 
   Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, ⁠where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said that what she called "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed. 
   She added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as ​a ​precaution had already been released.
fullText:
MOSCOW, Oct 6 (Reuters) - Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among people who had come ‌into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died ‌last week.

Authorities say the 28-year-old woman died on Friday from pneumonia of an as-yet unestablished origin, in ​a case that has prompted international concern, including from US President Donald Trump.

Rospotrebnadzor, the watchdog, said in a statement that no infectious diseases had been reported among the staff of the same plague research institute in Irkutsk over the past 10 ‌days and that extensive testing ⁠had found no microorganisms in the deceased woman's body linked to her work.

Elena Sofina, deputy head of the Shelekhov district near Irkutsk, ⁠where a local hospital was placed under quarantine, said that what she called "a dangerous diagnosis" had not been confirmed.

She added that 60% of those placed under quarantine as ​a ​precaution had already been released. Local media ​said around 200 people had previously ‌been quarantined.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov expressed appreciation for an offer of help on Monday from Trump, although without making clear if Moscow planned to accept it.

"It's always good when mutual assistance is offered," Peskov told reporters.

He said the public health watchdog was handling the situation and would provide further information as it became available.

Trump ‌on Monday described the situation as a "big problem ​for Russia". US Secretary of State Marco ​Rubio said on Tuesday it was ​incumbent on Moscow to share more information.

World Health Organization spokesperson ‌Christian Lindmeier said on Tuesday that Russian ​authorities had yet to ​officially respond to a WHO request for information about the death of the lab worker.

"All of the patient's contacts have been reportedly identified and ​are being monitored for illness, ‌and none to date have shown symptoms of illness," he said.

(Reporting ​by Vladimir Soldatkin, Anastasia Lyrchikova and Andrew Osborn; Writing by Maxim ​Rodionov and Mark TrevelyanEditing by Andrew Osborn )

title: Trump says his super PAC will now pay for ads after taxpayer-funded blitz
description:
President Donald Trump said Monday night that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a multimillion-dollar pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them. 
While he dismissed criticism of the ads as "a rather standard thing to do," he said he had decided to run them on his own dime rather than that of the U.S. government in a post on his social media platform.
"I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," Trump wrote, referring to his super PAC.
fullText:
The government has spent at least $2.5 million on the ads.

President Donald Trump said Monday night that he will no longer use taxpayer funds to pay for a multimillion-dollar pro-Trump ad blitz ahead of the midterm elections, saying his super PAC will now pay for them.

While he dismissed criticism of the ads as "a rather standard thing to do," he said he had decided to run them on his own dime rather than that of the U.S. government in a post on his social media platform.

"I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc," Trump wrote, referring to his super PAC.

The move comes after the U.S. government bankrolled a series of ads that aired nationally and heavily featured the president. One of the ads was a direct copy of a spot Trump's campaign ran in 2024.

A White House official confirmed to ABC News Monday night that MAGA Inc. will pay for ads moving forward but defended them as something previous administrations have used.

"Presidential Public service announcements are nothing new. Administrations of both parties have used public service announcements to explain policy and make the case for the nation’s direction," the official said.

Earlier Monday, Vice President JD Vance defended using taxpayer money to run the ads, claiming they are "public service announcements."

"They're not partisan. They're not -- you know, it's not like we're advocating for a particular candidate. We're trying to tell a story, I think, about how great the United States of America is," Vance said.

Trump defended the ads last week at an event in the Oval Office, saying they were "for the spirit of our country" and not a political endorsement for Republican candidates on the ballot this November or for his administration's policies.

"You have to understand; I'm not promoting a candidate. I'm not promoting myself because I'm not running for office. I'm promoting the country," Trump said.

"Now, if somebody said that that's wrong, I'll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country," he said.

Trump has implored Republican voters to "pretend" that he is on the ballot in the November midterm elections to boost voter turnout for GOP congressional candidates.

The federal government has spent at least $2.5 million to air the TV ads, according to an estimate from AdImpact, an advertising agency that analyzes ad spending across television.

A total of $20 million from the Department of Homeland Security's budget had been allocated for the effort.

Ethics watchdogs and several Congressional Democrats -- as well as some Republicans -- have said the ads are inappropriate. Some critics have said the ads could violate federal propaganda law.

Four ads have been aired over the last two weeks. One features Trump in monochrome, slowly walking down a hallway, describing "the final battle" against "the deep state," "the globalists," and "the sick political class that hates our country."

Another ad includes a montage of clips and images of Trump at events and rallies featuring onscreen text about the "largest tax cuts in history."

The latest ad, released last week, focuses on the U.S. war with Iran, now in its eighth month. Audio of Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth plays in the background as U.S. military footage, including unclassified strikes, is displayed.

The video in the ad appears to be the same as one played during the Republican midterm convention last month. And it played last Wednesday before Hegseth addressed 600 service members in his State of the Force speech at the Marine Corps base at Quantico, Virginia.

title: Trump approves firing squad execution for Fort Hood mass shooter Nidal Hasan
description:
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army officer and psychiatrist who killed 13 people and injured 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be executed by a U.S. Army firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday. 
“Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.
fullText:
Nidal Malik Hasan, a former Army officer and psychiatrist who killed 13 people and injured 32 others during a mass shooting at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009, will be executed by a U.S. Army firing squad, the Pentagon announced Monday.

"Secretary of War Pete Hegseth has recommended — and President Donald J. Trump has approved — death by U.S. Army firing squad for convicted terrorist Nidal Malik Hasan, the jihadist who opened fire on unarmed American soldiers at Fort Hood in 2009," Chief Pentagon Spokesman Sean Parnell announced. "He killed 13 people and wounded 32 others while shouting 'Allahu Akbar' during the attack.

"The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution," he continued. "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come."

If Hasan's execution is indeed carried out by a firing squad, it would mark the first such case for the service since Jan. 31, 1945, when Pvt. Eddie D. Slovik was executed by a U.S. Army firing squad in France for desertion during World War II.

The last death sentence carried out by the U.S. military was in 1961, when Army Pvt. John Bennett was executed by hanging at the gallows in Fort Leavenworth, Kansas, after he was convicted of raping and attempting to kill a young girl.

Hasan, who was born in northern Virginia, walked into a Fort Hood readiness processing center on Nov. 5, 2009, and opened fire using a semi-automatic handgun.

Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier.

Former Army Staff Sgt. Patrick Zeigler, a two-time combat veteran, was shot four times in the attack and spent nearly a year recovering in various hospitals.

"He looked me straight in the eyes as he pointed the gun at me, and a split second later, I'm on the floor with a hole in my head," he told the Killeen Daily Herald in 2023.

At his court-martial, Hasan, now 56, admitted to the shooting, and in 2013 said he carried out the attack in support of the Taliban.

At the time, Hasan requested a delay in court proceedings so he could ready a new legal strategy that would show he acted "in defense of others."

Asked by presiding Judge Col. Tara Osborn who he was defending, Hasan replied, "The leadership of the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan, the Taliban."

Hasan was convicted by a military jury in August 2013, which recommended he be sentenced to death.

He was subsequently transferred to Fort Leavenworth, where he has been incarcerated on death row.

Jonathan Lehrfeld contributed to this report.

title: Trump expands access to tax-exempt diesel fuel with an executive order
description:
US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday to expand access to tax-exempt diesel that ‌he unveiled from a rally stage in Nebraska. 
   High diesel prices, which shot to a ‌record of about $6.50 a gallon last month, are a risk to Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm US elections ​in which control of Congress is at stake. Trump's Republican Party currently holds a narrow majority in the Senate and House of Representatives. 
   Prices for the fuel integral to trucking goods have risen in response to the US-Israeli war on Iran and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with the conflicts having led to ‌attacks on refineries in the Middle ⁠East and Russia.
fullText:
GRAND ISLAND, Nebraska, Oct 5 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump signed an executive order on Monday to expand access to tax-exempt diesel that ‌he unveiled from a rally stage in Nebraska.

High diesel prices, which shot to a ‌record of about $6.50 a gallon last month, are a risk to Trump ahead of the November 3 midterm US elections ​in which control of Congress is at stake. Trump's Republican Party currently holds a narrow majority in the Senate and House of Representatives.

Prices for the fuel integral to trucking goods have risen in response to the US-Israeli war on Iran and the Russian invasion of Ukraine, with the conflicts having led to ‌attacks on refineries in the Middle ⁠East and Russia.

Trump said the directive will waive the off-road requirement for tax-free diesel and allow anyone to buy the red dye diesel fuel that ⁠is used by the agriculture industry and by some off-road vehicles.

"We are not going to need it long, I hope," Trump said of the waiver.

The order released by the White House directs the treasury secretary, in ​consultation ​with the Pentagon chief, "to defer payment of the federal ​excise tax imposed for on-road use of ‌dyed diesel fuel for the remainder of the year without interest or penalties, and to explore pathways to eliminate the obligation to pay the deferred taxes."

It also directs the US agriculture secretary to "ensure farmers' access to dyed diesel in high-demand areas" while asking the transportation secretary to coordinate with states, industry leadership, and labor organizations on access to dyed diesel.

G7 countries announced last week that they ‌would release 100 million barrels of diesel, after pressure ​from Trump who had considered banning US exports of the ​fuel. But it was not clear how ​much of that release would be entirely new supplies or compliance with a ‌global agreement in March.

Trump's approval rating held ​at a record-low 32% ​in recent days, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday, with Americans most concerned about the high cost of living, spurred by soaring gasoline and diesel prices due to the ​US war on Iran.

title: Russia disputes plague report as Trump offers U.S. help
description:
President Donald Trump said the US was ready to help Russia with the reported plague case (Brendan SMIALOWSKI)
Russia on Monday sought to downplay reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, even as President Donald Trump said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and offered US help.
Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.
"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.
"We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can."
The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.
fullText:
Russia on Monday sought to downplay reports that a laboratory technician had died of plague, even as President Donald Trump said Washington was closely monitoring the situation and offered US help.

Reports on Friday that pneumonic plague had killed a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working for the anti-plague institute in Siberia's Irkutsk region, sparked alarm.

"We're looking at it very strongly, we just heard about it," Trump told reporters at the White House when asked what Washington was going to do about the risk of plague coming from Russia.

"We'll help them, we'll help them as much as we can."

The Russian news outlet People of Baikal, citing unnamed sources close to the regional security services, said the dead woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube.

Other media reported a possible link between her death and a lab accident at the facility.

As many as 200 people with whom she may have had contact were under quarantine, the People of Baikal outlet added, without elaborating.

But Russian officials stressed that postmortem tests had not detected the disease.

Irkutsk Regional Governor Igor Kobzev said Monday that a special expert commission inspection in the region had found that "the cause of death was pneumonia of undetermined aetiology".

He said on Telegram that Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor had determined, following tests, that "no microorganisms linked to the young woman's professional work were found in her biological samples".

He added that there had been "no new cases of staff from the anti-plague institute seeking medical attention" since the woman's death.

Kobzev said the sanitary-epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was "stable".

"The situation remains under our control and that of the experts."

Asked about the situation on Monday, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters to "rely on Rospotrebnadzor's official statements rather than... rumours and speculations".

Plague is a bacterial disease that can occur in several forms, including pneumonic plague, which is the most contagious type and can be transmitted by respiratory means. Bubonic plague is transmitted by infected fleas.

Pneumonic plague can be fatal if not treated early, according to the World Health Organization.

The reports will be closely watched in Washington, where memories of the Covid-19 pandemic that started in Trump's first term are still fresh.

Trump has strongly backed the theory that the disease was due to a leak from a laboratory in Wuhan, China.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said his country was monitoring the Russia situation but saw no "cause for alarm".

"There's very limited travel between the US and Russia, obviously, but like anything else, something like that gets out, it could quickly spread," Rubio told reporters before taking off for a visit to Iceland.

"So we're watching and monitoring it closely. I don't think it's cause for alarm, but it is cause for focus and a cause to just keep an eye on it. And we're doing that."

Experts said the reported response in Russia appeared "proportionate".

"It appears that measures are being implemented to quarantine any potential contacts and prevent any onward transmission," Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology, Imperial College London, said in a commentary.

title: Sen. Tillis calls deciding vote for Hegseth the 'biggest regret' of his career
description:
— Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the “biggest regret of my career” and that he also “should’ve stopped” Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump’s second term. 
In “How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents,” to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be “the lone voice in the wilderness” preventing Trump’s nominees from confirmation.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Republican Sen. Thom Tillis says in a new book that his deciding vote to confirm Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in January 2025 is the "biggest regret of my career" and that he also "should've stopped" Robert F. Kennedy Jr. from becoming Health and Human Services secretary in the early days of President Donald Trump's second term.

In "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents," to be published Tuesday, the North Carolina senator defends his decision at the time to not be "the lone voice in the wilderness" preventing Trump's nominees from confirmation. But Tillis makes clear he was always skeptical of allegations about Hegseth's turbulent management style, treatment of women and excessive drinking. Hegseth denied all the allegations.

"I know for a fact that there are others like me," Tillis writes, "Republicans who agreed to go along with the early demands of the Trump team no matter how ridiculous they were, believing that failing to do so would mean the end of their political career, and who now see that things have gone way too far."

He writes that he can count at least 30 of his GOP colleagues who have "expressed reservations (to put it mildly) about many of the president's actions in private. Then, when the reporters showed up with their cameras and microphones, they'd have nothing but nice things to say."

Tillis, who announced last year that he would not run for reelection in a "breaking point" with the president on his sweeping tax and spending cuts package, is publishing the book in his final months in office. He joins a long list of Republicans who have ratcheted up their public denunciations of Trump once they had less to lose politically.

Still, Tillis mostly deflects full blame from Trump, saying, "my beef is not with him, but the idiots he's got working for him." He calls the president "an amazing political talent."

At the same time, he warns of a slippery slope toward authoritarianism and urges his colleagues to "wake up" and push back on Trump more often, for their own political good. Executive overreach, he says, doesn't work and sooner or later, "comes back to bite the majority party in the ass."

Tillis also predicts a "bloodbath" for Republicans in November's midterm elections.

"All along, we've had multiple chances to get off the path and avoid the giant bronze monster chasing us down," he writes.

The book is filled with cuss words and condemnations. He criticizes Trump's tariffs, the aggressive immigration raids that Tillis says were an effort to "intentionally sow disorder" and the Iran war, which he initially supported. He said the war can only end with a coalition of willing nations and if Trump gets "Pete Hegseth the hell out of the way."

Tillis pushed Hegseth's confirmation vote late into the evening on Jan. 24, 2025, as he weighed his decision, talking to the White House, people who had worked with Hegseth and Hegseth himself. In the end, he said he couldn't corroborate the worst allegations and would support Hegseth's confirmation. His vote brought the total to 50-50, and Vice President JD Vance broke the tie.

On his vote for Kennedy, Tillis writes that "I guess it's easy to say now, but I'm the one who has to live with that vote and all the havoc Kennedy's tenure has caused the country as a result."

On both votes, he says he didn't want to be the deciding factor.

"I had no intention of letting my colleagues outsource their courage to me while they pretended to go along with the questionable nomination President Trump had put forward," he writes.

If you oppose Trump on everything, "you lose all influence," Tillis says. "If you oppose him and lose, you are in even worse shape."

He strongly criticizes several of Trump's other initial picks for the Cabinet in the book, including former Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

Tillis's surprise announcement in June 2025 that he wouldn't be running for reelection came as he escalated criticism against Trump and his " Big Beautiful Bill " of tax and spending cuts. Trump attacked Tillis on social media after the senator said he couldn't support the bill's cuts to Medicaid. Tillis says he thought to himself, "I'm done."

"Everyone reaches a breaking point," he writes.

He texted the president asking him to look for his replacement in the Senate, to which Trump replied "I am! DJT."

In May 2026, Trump again attacked Tillis, calling him a "QUITTER!" on social media, among other insults.

Tillis ends the book with a profanity-laced text he sent to the president in response.

"I care if you fail and right now we are failing," Tillis wrote to Trump.

title: 4 ways the midterm elections could turn out, with a month to go
description:
Democrats are heading into the last month of the midterm elections campaign with ambitions going deeper and deeper into red territory, while Republicans are grim about their hopes of holding on to either chamber of Congress.
Historically, the opposition party almost always makes gains in the midterms, and President Donald Trump is less popular than ever. His support has weakened especially with independents in high-quality polls and among swing demographics that propelled his 2024 majority.

fullText:
Democrats are heading into the last month of the midterm elections campaign with ambitions going deeper and deeper into red territory, while Republicans are grim about their hopes of holding on to either chamber of Congress.

Historically, the opposition party almost always makes gains in the midterms, and President Donald Trump is less popular than ever. His support has weakened especially with independents in high-quality polls and among swing demographics that propelled his 2024 majority.

Republicans have also tended to underperform when Trump isn't on the ballot because more consistent voters have shifted toward the Democrats. More Democrats voted in this year's primaries - a sign that they are also more likely to turn out now, with early and mail voting already underway in 43 states leading up to Election Day on Nov. 3.

The Democrats' lead in national and battleground polls has expanded since Labor Day. There are reasons to suspect polls could be overestimating Democrats' strength, though surveys did not systematically favor Democrats in the last two midterms.

Republicans' main advantage is money. GOP campaigns and allies are outspending Democrats in almost all the most contested races, thanks in large part to more than $180 million that has been pumped in from Trump's war chest since Labor Day.

The outcome will define the remainder of Trump's presidency - the fate of his legislative ambitions and the pressure of oversight investigations. It will also immediately set the stage for the 2028 presidential primaries, with both parties' hopefuls reading the results for clues to the electorate's mood.

Here are four possible ways the midterms could broadly shake out.

In the House, Republicans hold the slimmest of majorities, with 218 seats (and one independent who caucuses with them) to the Democrats' 214. The GOP is on defense in 16 seats rated toss-ups by the Cook Political Report, compared with six for Democrats. On Sept. 25, Cook shifted 15 races toward the Democrats and projected them to take over the House.

Anticipating a favorable environment, Democrats went into the cycle planning to expand the House battlefield by recruiting competitive candidates to run in typically safe GOP districts held by incumbents unaccustomed to tough races or dragged down in scandals. On Friday, they continued widening their targets, adding eight districts that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024. They added six more races on Monday, including seats in Arkansas and Tennessee and a Nevada district that backed Trump by 14 points. The latest additions bring their total targets to 46.

If Democrats win the popular vote by 10 points this year - their current average lead in polls - they would pick up a projected 33 seats, according to Mindset, a Washington advisory firm. That would place this year's gains between the Democratic pickups in 2006 (31 seats) and 2018 (40 seats).

"Democrats are on offense; Republicans are running scared - even in deep-red territory," said Rep. Suzan DelBene (Washington), chair of the House Democrats' campaign arm. "Voters are fed up with Republicans' broken promises and ready for change in Congress."

In the Senate, Republicans hold a 53-47 majority and were favored to keep control earlier this year.

Now, most polls put Democrats ahead in the most contested races: Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Michigan, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas. They're more strongly favored to win North Carolina, where former governor Roy Cooper (D) leads former Republican National Committee chairman Michael Whatley, and Georgia, where Rep. Mike Collins (R) hasn't come close to catching Sen. Jon Ossoff (D). On Friday, the main Republican Senate super PAC canceled its remaining spending in North Carolina.

Beyond the battlegrounds, Republicans have shown concern about incumbents in Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, and Nebraska, which Trump won by 20 points in 2024. Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kansas), an obstetrician, is under fire for his history of suing patients to collect unpaid bills, leading to some arrests. He faces megachurch pastor Adam Hamilton (D). Nebraska independent Dan Osborn has been slamming Sen. Pete Ricketts (R) for pardoning a man convicted of sexual assault when he was governor.

In the most extreme scenario, some political professionals imagine the wave wiping out Sen. Darline Graham (R-South Carolina) or Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida).

The Senate does not as consistently turn against the president - Republicans added two seats in the upper chamber in 2018. This year's map has more GOP-held seats in contention, but taking the majority would require the Democrats to hold Georgia and Michigan, pick up North Carolina and Maine, plus win two out of 12 seats in states that Trump won by at least 13 points.

In the House, Democrats need a net gain of only three seats. But across decades, partisan gerrymandering has steadily shrunk the battlefield, so even an electoral swing of similar magnitude to past cycles might not flip as many seats.

This cycle, Republicans tilted the field further in their direction by redrawing congressional maps ahead of the customary once-a-decade redistricting. Republicans hoped to move 16 districts to the right with new maps in Texas (five districts), Florida (four), Ohio (two), Alabama, Louisiana, Missouri, North Carolina and Tennessee (one each). Democrats responded with five districts in California, and courts overturned the Missouri map and added a Democratic-leaning seat in Utah, cutting the Republicans' theoretical edge to nine.

But many of those redrawn seats are shaping up to be less solid than Republicans had hoped. Democrats are still contesting four redrawn seats in Texas and another four in Florida. They hope to keep one or two affected districts in Ohio (held by Reps. Marcy Kaptur and Greg Landsman), plus the one in North Carolina (Rep. Don Davis).

"People want to make predictions, but there's a lot of toss-up races that are not decided yet," Republican pollster John McLaughlin said. "The sides are forming where the Democratic/anti-Republican vote is coming together and Republicans are losing the ability to recover swing voters. That's concerning."

In the previous midterms of 2022, the roles were reversed: Republicans were confident the unpopular sitting president would sweep their candidates into power despite their flaws, and were dismayed when that wave failed to materialize. Now, they are hoping for a similar dynamic, only the other way around.

If Republicans pull an upset, they'll be able to thank the Senate map that puts them mostly on their home turf and gerrymandering for padding their cushion in the House. The polls would have to be significantly off, which could be because Democrats were more eager to answer the phone, Republicans were less likely to participate, or pollsters misjudged who would turn out to vote.

Trump political adviser Chris LaCivita summed up the Republicans' path to victory as: "money, message, motivation and the president's ability to defy conventional wisdom."

Republicans outspent Democrats in every Senate battleground in September and also led in future reservations though Election Day, according to media tracker AdImpact.

Republicans are also hoping to benefit in races where further-left Democrats won their primaries. Those Democrats include Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan and House candidates William Lawrence in Michigan and Randy Villegas in California.

The GOP's midterms convention and Trump's stump speeches have sought to portray the Democrats as extreme and tie the entire party to self-described socialists who won in some areas.

And as much as Democrats want to make the race about Trump (and he does, too), at least some Republicans may be able to outperform his unpopularity. Candidates from Iowa to Florida have started removing references to Trump from their websites and breaking with the president on immigration and the Iran war.

Elections are run at the local level, with no role for the federal government. The Trump administration has made multiple attempts to change voting procedures for the midterms, but those efforts were held up in court or died in Congress.

"It has been a roller coaster," Eric Fey, the Democratic elections director in St. Louis, said at a recent meeting of elections officials.

Each election cycle features emergency litigation over mishaps at voting locations (often resulting in extended hours), recounts in close races and post-election audits. Administrators and law enforcement officials are also on the lookout for cyberattacks or disruptions such as bomb threats. They conduct drills and simulations to anticipate how things could go wrong and practice how to respond.

"The threat landscape, as we view it this year, is cyber, physical, logistical, reputational and somewhat emergent legal," said Michael Moore, the chief information security officer for the Arizona secretary of state's office. "We design exercises to give election officials the most miserable Election Day we can possibly imagine. That way, when they actually have an election day, they're prepared for everything."

This year, election administrators are especially concerned about interference from the federal government. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has said the administration has no plans to send immigration officers to polls, while FBI Director Kash Patel would not rule out sending his agents to voting sites.

"While I anticipate that we likely will have monitors and there could be incidents at or around voting locations, we're going to make sure that we have boots on the ground to make sure that voters are not disrupted in that process and that they can cast a ballot," said Dean Logan, the registrar-recorder and county clerk for Los Angeles County, the country's largest election jurisdiction.

Monica Gordon, the clerk in Cook County, Illinois (home to Chicago), added: "We're moving forward as usual, but we plan for anything. Our contingencies have contingencies."

Right-wing activists have called for Trump to take more severe steps, such as trying to claim emergency powers over elections. Trump has repeatedly challenged the legitimacy of elections he and his party lost. Congressional Democrats and allied lawyers have also prepared research and drills to be ready for any attempts to use federal power to interfere with the results, as Trump attempted after losing in 2020.

"A lot of people would say that we need to just go rogue and declare this radical emergency," Tina Peters, a former Colorado county clerk who was released on parole in June after serving some of her sentence for tampering with voting equipment, said Wednesday during a meeting of online activists. "There are already orders and laws in place that allow them to do what they need to do."

title: Tejano singer trying to win back Latinos who voted for Trump, one quinceañera at a time
description: Bobby Pulido pictured for the Guardian in September 2026.Photograph: Brenda Bazán/The...
fullText:
It took all of two minutes for Bobby Pulido's electoral stealth weapon to come into play. The Tejano music star turned Democratic congressional candidate had barely begun canvassing in the high school football stadium in Edinburg, Texas, when a 15-year-old girl came rushing up to him.

"Señor Pulido! Señor Pulido!" she cried. A few months ago, she told him, he had made a surprise appearance at her quinceañera, the coming-of-age girls' 15th birthday party that is a rite of passage in these US borderlands.

He had serenaded her with Desvelado, his blockbuster love song, which though released three decades ago retains a treasured place in Tejano – that is Hispanic Texan – culture.

The brief encounter gave a glimpse into one of the key dynamics of Pulido's bid to flip Texas's 15th congressional district. He calls it the "quinceañera strategy".

The tactic was handed to him, inadvertently, by his rival, the two-term incumbent Republican congresswoman Monica De La Cruz. In March, she posted a video deriding her opponent as a lowly quinceañera singer.

The election, she said, "isn't about who you want performing at your niece's quinceañera. It's about who you trust with your family's future."

Pulido pounced. He counter-posted his own video in which he accused De La Cruz of belittling a cherished local tradition and encouraged families in the district planning a quinceañera to invite him. "I'd be honored to stop by and celebrate with you," he said.

Within 24 hours, Pulido's campaign had been inundated with over 1,000 invitations. By the time the Guardian went canvassing with him in September, that number had surpassed 5,000.

He has now performed at 81 quinceañeras and counting. Each one is attended by scores of family and friends, most of whom are eligible voters and many of whom livestream the event on their smartphones, broadcasting it to additional scores of eligible voters.

"She presented us with an opportunity for a very unique kind of field plan," Abel Prado, Pulido's campaign manager, said.

Pulido, 53, is hoping to convert the quinceañera strategy and the rest of the tireless retail politics that he is doing into a winning political formula. His mission: to take back the congressional seat, and in the process both help the national Democratic party regain control of the US House and teach it a lesson or two about Mexican American politics.

It's not just that flipping Texas 15 could give Democrats the edge they need to take back control of the House of Representatives. The stakes are also huge for the Rio Grande valley itself, the overwhelmingly Hispanic border region in south Texas that for over a century was solidly Democratic but swung hard for Donald Trump in 2024.

Trump won the district, which is 81% Mexican American and which runs for over 300 miles from the border to San Antonio, by 18 points.

How Pulido fares in the November midterm elections could have ripple effects for fellow Democrat James Talarico's currently neck-and-neck fight for a US Senate seat against the state's scandal-ridden Republican attorney general, Ken Paxton. Talarico's chance of success is also heavily dependent on Latino turnout.

And in the widest sense, Pulido's message has bearings on the national Democratic party as it debates how to counter the dramatic inroads made by Trump two years ago when he smashed records and garnered 55% of Texas's Hispanic vote.

Pulido made sure to display his Tejano stripes as he strutted around the Edinburg stadium, while cheerleaders and a marching band filled the night air with colour and noise. Dressed in jeans and denim shirt, cowboy boots and hat, he moved confidently through the crowd of high-school football fans.

He shook the hand of everyone he met, chatting to supporters on both sides of the bleachers – a calculated move as both high school teams, Sabrecats and Yellowjackets, are in the 15th district. (The Sabrecats won 31-14.)

And yet almost everyone in attendance was too young to vote – so what was the point?

"To win re-election," Pulido quipped, without missing a beat. Then, with more reflection, he added: "If you treat kids good, their parents will like you."

Pulido has a catchphrase: "Any occasion, big or small." He means it. The football game was the 526th campaign event he had attended in person. His record is 12 such stops in a single day.

When Pulido sat down to talk with the Guardian, he emphasised accessibility was a critical element of his campaign. It's his answer, he said, to the increasingly polarised left-right media bubbles that keep voters divided.

"The only way I can break through is to actually get in front of people the old-fashioned way. Then people can hear me. They can look me in the eye, and decide for themselves whether I'm full of shit or not."

Direct connection with voters also allows Pulido, who has roots stretching back seven generations in the Rio Grande valley, to play his ace card: his near-universal name recognition in the region.

Desvelado ("sleepless") was his first, and is still his biggest, hit – the 1995 album of the same name went platinum, and the song has been played 615m times on Spotify. He has won two Latin Grammys for best Tejano album; the day before we met he celebrated yet another nomination for the award, for Una Tuya, Una Mía, Vol 2.

If the massive popularity of Desvelado gives him an entree with younger and middle-aged Tejanos, he can count on his father to grab the attention of older voters. José Roberto Pulido, 75, is a Tejano music star in his own right, having enjoyed a large local following in the 1970s and 80s.

In Pulido's analysis, Trump lured so many of these Tejano voters away from the Democratic party in 2024 because he spoke to their longing for the American dream. There's a popular phrase in the valley: "We know we're broke, but don't tell us we're poor."

Pulido said: "If you're poor, you've already lost; if you're broke, you could still make it one day. Trump kind of won because of that message. 'Look at me, I'm rich, and some of my richness will transfer to you' – that was music to people's ears."

Trump's promise to close the US-Mexico border also spoke to many people in the valley. The disruption caused by record numbers of undocumented immigrants crossing into the US during the Biden administration was especially felt in this frontier zone, and many Tejano US citizens bridled against it despite their own immigrant heritage.

"Under Biden, the border was chaotic," Pulido said. "The tent cities, the visible hardship, so many coming across."

Since the return of Trump to the White House, however, Pulido believes that the president has squandered much of that goodwill. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made Texas the ground zero of its mass deportation efforts, notably so given the central position the state commands within Trump's Maga universe.

Figures compiled by the Deportation Data Project show that ICE made 12,086 arrests in July in Texas. That was almost twice the number in the next most intensely targeted states, Florida (7,405) and California (6,464).

Pulido is convinced that Trump will pay a price in November for this blanket assault on Texas immigrants. "People are angry, ICE enforcement is splitting up families and spreading fear. And it's hurting our economy. There's not a building in the Rio Grande valley that was put up without immigrant hands. None."

He added: "There is a reckoning coming, that's for sure. I see it. We've polled it. People don't like what the Republican party is doing."

The most recent survey of the 15th district, from Texas Southern University, puts Pulido five points ahead of De La Cruz (50% to 45%). Among Latino likely voters, the gap widens to 25 points (60% to 35%).

"This election is showing that the Trump bubble is burst," the co-author of the opinion poll, Mark Jones, professor of political science at Rice University, said. "We did see a temporary shift towards Trump among Latino voters, but now we're coming back to a more standard status quo."

The Guardian spoke to several 15th district voters who two years ago enthusiastically cast their ballots for Trump yet who have grown disaffected and disillusioned.

Yajaira Martinez, 43, is a naturalized citizen who came to the US from Mexico when she was six. In 2024, she voted for Trump because she believed his promises about bringing down prices and improving the economy, and because she supported his desire for a stronger border.

She heard him pledge to remove undocumented immigrants with criminal records. "If you want to take the criminals out of the country, by all means go ahead," she said.

But she did not expect the ICE dragnet of hardworking people trying to make a go for their families. She knows several people who have been deported even though they had legitimate work permits.

"ICE is breaking the law, they are assaulting, they are chasing down. They are terrorising. This administration doesn't care about anybody's rights."

Juan Cantu, 66, was born in Mexico but lives in the US, and as a naturalized citizen is entitled to vote. He makes an income both as a cabinet maker and rancher.

He voted for Trump in 2024 because he was fed up with Democrats talking about social issues such as abortion and trans people using women's bathrooms, and he thought Trump would be on his side as un trabajador, a worker.

But he's been appalled as he watches "the politics of Trump spinning out of control, harming so many working people". The Iran war, which he said he does not understand, and tariffs have pushed the diesel that powers his tractor to $6 a gallon, and that's a problem.

As for Pulido, Cantu likes his father's Tejano music. "That's the music of my época," he said. And he warms to the candidate's politics. "From what I've heard, he wants to help the poor, the working people."

Juan Pablo Lopez, 41, a first-generation Mexican American born in the US, is the owner of a real estate and construction company in McAllen. He voted for Trump because he liked the way he spoke the language of business.

In the past year, though, it's turned sour for Lopez. He estimates that about 60 of his co-workers and friends have disappeared, rounded up by ICE and detained then deported.

He said he had come to conclusion that Trump is not the friend of Tejanos. "Everybody here believed in him, and instead of helping us, he's hurting us."

As for his vote in November, it's complicated. Lopez said he likes Pulido. "I was born and raised with his music. He's a family guy, and I like that he's very conservative."

What he doesn't like is that Pulido is running as a Democrat, a party he thinks has a "Robin Hood mentality". "They take from the rich to give to the poor – let's give everybody food stamps, let's make sure everybody's on housing. I'm a hardworking American."

That leaves him in a bind. "I'm faced with a very hard decision of who I'm going to vote for. I don't want to vote Democrat, but look at what Trump has done to us."

It's Pulido's challenge to overcome the hesitation of voters like Lopez. He must harness their patent anger towards Trump's handling of immigration and the economy, and persuade them that not all Democrats are leftist progressives.

As he faces this challenge, Pulido is careful to emphasise his conservative convictions while avoiding talking in party political terms. The race is not about Democrat versus Republican, but about Bobby versus Monica.

"I do not mention blue waves. Not ever."

There is a populist side to Pulido's politics that bears comparison to Bernie Sanders. He denounces "crony capitalism" and demands that corporate money is removed from US elections.

Pulido doesn't have health insurance because "it's not worth it".

"I should not feel obligated to feed those monsters. Health insurance companies get away with it, and doctors can't even be doctors any more," he said.

Beneath the populist patina, his innate cultural conservatism – typical of this border region – is glaringly apparent. He is a man of faith, and is personally opposed to abortion though his policy is that he would not impose his views on anybody else: "Pro-life is a choice too. It's my choice," he said.

He opposes restrictions on oil and gas extraction, including fracking, as they account for a significant proportion of the valley's jobs. He wants the border to remain locked down even after Trump has gone, though he wants that to be done humanely.

There's no doubting his support for the second amendment. He named his son Remington, after the Remington 700 bolt-action rifle that he loves.

If you described a politician with that set of convictions to a person in Brooklyn or Santa Monica they might assume he were a moderate Republican. So what makes him a Democrat?

"I'm a Democrat because I lead with my democratic heart," he said. "I understand that there are people out there who need help, and that it's my obligation as a Catholic and as a Christian to do what I can to help my fellow neighbor."

In all this, there is an implicit criticism of the national leadership of the Democratic party and what he regards as its coastal elite prejudices.

"In music, you have to know your audience. I'm smart enough to know that you don't take a symphonic orchestra to the dancehall – people want to dance. But that's what my party is doing, taking the east coast and west coast politics of the liberal elites and bringing them to where they do not resonate."

Warming to the theme, he said: "What plays well in New York City likely won't play well among Democratic voters in the valley. The party has become too one-size-fits-all, and that's a big mistake."

His main takeaway from his months running for congressional office is that Democrats "let other people define us".

"When I first told people in this district that I was running as a Democrat, their automatic assumption was that I was going to take away their guns, that I was for trans in women's sports, that I was going to take away their oil and gas jobs," he said. "That's the narrative they were fed by Republicans."

As the 3 November election gets closer, and the temperature of the race rises, De La Cruz has tried to stall Pulido's advance by hitting him with negative attack ads casting him as a "corrupt liberal celebrity". In particular, she has focused on revelations that an accordionist in Pulido's band who played on the recording of Desvelado later became a registered sex offender.

De La Cruz has accused Pulido of "endangering our families". He counters that he only discovered his band member's sex crimes record years later.

The Republican has also charged Pulido with demeaning voters, basing the claim on a 2020 video that has resurfaced in which he is seen laughing as a comedy host made remarks about women's bodies following childbirth and on past social media posts in which he used racist and homophobic slurs. Pulido has admitted that some of his comments crossed the line and apologised for them. But he argues that De La Cruz has supported a president who has repeatedly attacked women's appearances.

So far there is insufficient data from opinion polls to know whether the mud is sticking.

Republican efforts to win congressional seats in south Texas through redistricting may also backfire on De La Cruz. The 15th district was redrawn with the aim of preserving her lead while at the same time attempting to flip neighboring seats from the Democrats.

As a result almost two-thirds of the voters in the reconfigured 15th district are new to De La Cruz, with many voters having little or no idea who she is.

That matters when she is up against someone with almost universal name recognition like Pulido. "When I saw the map, I was very happy," he said with a grin.

Asked to comment on Pulido's political record and the state of the race, De La Cruz's campaign manager, James Shook, described Pulido as "a silver-spooned scumbag who enabled a sex predator".

"Anyone starstruck by this pedo-protecting loser should be ashamed of themselves," he said in the statement.

There is a bittersweetness to the looming election for Pulido. He is potentially poised to pull off a historic victory that would send him to Washington where a whole new political life would await him.

But it would mark the end of his other life as a Tejano musician. Last year he embarked on a farewell tour, and just before we met his final performance was announced.

It will take place in Edinburg, 17 days before the election. He's calling it La Última Desvelada.

title: Ex-Army secretary who quit Pentagon confirms clashes with Hegseth in interview

fullText:
Former Army secretary Dan Driscoll has given his first interview since resigning from the Pentagon in September after clashing with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Driscoll is just one of a series of high profile departures since Hegseth took over, with the secretary carrying out a purge so substantial it reportedly even raised President Donald Trump’s concerns.

Speaking to Rolling Stone, Driscoll acknowledged the pair had disagreements on a number of issues, without going into specifics.

“Once he makes a decision, there’s nothing I can do about it. I don’t have to like it,” he said of Hegseth. “But I think it’s unfair to describe our relationship so flatly – that every interaction was bad, or that we disagreed on everything.

“If you polled us, we probably agreed on more than 50 percent of things. What’s been reported is all the things we disagree on.

“I’ll never talk about our private conversations but we were both very passionate about our positions, and I would advocate as strongly as I possibly could – knowing I’m talking to my boss, and the final decision-maker.”

Driscoll said his role had been “to advocate as hard as I could for leaders who I thought were good.”

An Iraq War veteran, tech investor and former adviser to Vice President JD Vance – whom he befriended while they were contemporaries at Yale Law School – Driscoll is characterized in the piece as a keen modernizer of the U.S. military, interested in innovation and ensuring the Armed Forces had the equipment necessary to meet the challenges of a 21st century battlefield.

While Hegseth was also interested in making changes to the operation of the military, reports suggest he has been concerned about instilling a “warfighter” mentality in the troops and focussing on appearance.

Driscoll, the youngest person ever to hold his position after sailing through his confirmation hearing in the Senate in February 2025, recounts how he approached Hegseth early on with what he considered a “gift” – his close friendship with Vance – which he believed would help the Pentagon get what it needed from the White House.

But, the magazine reported: “Hegseth blew up at him… telling Driscoll that he needed to go through his office before reaching out to the White House, creating a tension between the two men.”

The friction worsened as Hegseth dismissed more and more top generals and admirals, culminating in the removal of Gen. Randy George and then Gen. Christopher Donahue, two men with whom Driscoll had found common cause in pursuing his modernizing agenda.

Driscoll reached the end of his tether in late August and informed President Donald Trump of his intention to resign, reportedly telling the commander-in-chief that he was leaving because Hegseth had fired everyone working towards the goal he held dear.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, responded to The Independent’s inquiry about Driscoll’s comments by calling Rolling Stone “a fake news rag regurgitating months-old false narratives in an attempt to stay relevant to their ever-dwindling audience” and alleging that its interview “is riddled with made-up claims regarding Secretary Hegseth’s historic achievements and transformative leadership.”

“Since Day One, Secretary Hegseth has focused on modernization across every branch of our Armed Forces and has moved with urgency to deliver on President Trump’s vision of Peace Through Strength,” Parnell said.

“From slashing bureaucracy, to untying the hands of our warfighters, to re-energizing our defense industrial base, Secretary Hegseth has been a generational Secretary for the Pentagon. With President Trump and Secretary Hegseth at the helm, our military will remain the greatest fighting force on the planet.”

Driscoll was praised by White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly when he left his post as “highly effective in advancing President Trump’s agenda to Make America Strong Again at the Department of the Army by providing outstanding leadership during historic military operations, restoring an emphasis on readiness and lethality, assisting with negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, and more.”

"The United States Army is more powerful than ever thanks to his work alongside the Commander-in-Chief and Secretary of War,” she added.

fullText:
The US Strategic Petroleum Reserve (SPR) dropped by almost 800,000 barrels last week, and the Trump administration moved forward with plans to sell another 40 million barrels in the coming months.

New data released on Monday by the US Department of Energy showed the US energy backstop sitting at 283 million barrels, down from 283.77 million the week prior.

That leaves about two weeks of US oil consumption in the reserve amid widespread worries about global stockpiles, which the head of Saudi Arabia's state producer on Monday called "scarily thin."

Amin Nasser, chief executive of Saudi Aramco, added at an Energy Intelligence Forum in London on Monday that releasing stockpiles will buy economies some time but won't fix the imbalances that have developed between supply and demand.

Yet these withdrawals in the US could soon accelerate after the Trump administration unveiled a request for bids from companies to buy up to 40 million barrels of crude oil from the SPR, with the aim of having the companies return those supplies "with additional premium barrels." The solicitation process is ongoing, and it's unclear if companies will agree to those terms.

The Trump administration continues to wrestle with high energy prices, less than a month before the midterm elections, and is reportedly preparing an executive order to expand access ‌to tax-exempt diesel, with the president confirming on Monday afternoon, "I'll be helping [farmers] with diesel."

In recent days, G7 countries — including the US — announced a new set of plans to release up to 100 million barrels of emergency fuel, including "a frontloaded substantial diesel release."

A White House official told Yahoo Finance that Trump intends to follow through on a commitment to release a total of 172 million barrels from the SPR, which was announced earlier this year.

The US energy backstop already sits at the lowest level seen since October of 1982, and a withdrawal of another 40 million barrels would put the reserve at its lowest level since records began being kept earlier in 1982, as the backstop was still coming online under President Ronald Reagan.

For his part, President Trump continues to project confidence that the US reserves will be quickly refilled. He told a crowd in Alabama over the weekend that, because of an energy deal with Venezuela, "we're going to be filling up very shortly our strategic reserves for nothing."

Experts say that, despite Trump's promises, refilling the reserves will be a complex and far-from-free process that could take years.

fullText:

Leavitt, 29, who will provide commentary across the Fox News lineup, starts on Nov. 1. She most recently served as the 36th White House press secretary during President Donald Trump’s second administration, from January 2025 until August 2026.

We look forward to her providing our audience with authentic and sharp insight across all FOX News Media platforms," Scott said in a statement.

TRUMP SAYS KAROLINE LEAVITT WILL LEAVE WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY ROLE, BECOME OUTSIDE ADVISOR

Leavitt added, "I am grateful for the opportunity to continue appearing on Fox News Channel as an official member of the extraordinary team at FOX News Media. I look forward to bringing my unique perspective from my experience as White House press secretary, along with the same energy and candor that defined my tenure, to Fox’s millions of viewers across their many platforms."

Leavitt served as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., before joining Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and later becoming the youngest White House press secretary in history. She quickly developed a reputation as an unwavering messenger of the president’s agenda.

As the administration’s chief spokesperson, she regularly addressed the White House press corps and represented the administration on a wide range of domestic and foreign policy issues.

DAVID MARCUS: KAROLINE LEAVITT’S LASTING LEGACY IS OPENING THE WHITE HOUSE TO INDIE PRESS
