title: Supreme Court will review Trump admin.'s mandatory immigrant detention policy
description:
— The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for immigrants as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.
The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.
The case will test a key pillar of the Trump administration's hard-line immigration agenda.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for immigrants as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.

The justices will consider whether immigrants who have been living in the U.S. have a right to a hearing to determine if they should remain detained while challenging their possible deportation.

The case will test a key pillar of the Trump administration's hard-line immigration agenda.

Most appeals courts to have considered the issue have found that it violates federal law to detain immigrants, including those living in the U.S. illegally, without a bond hearing. Those decisions conflict with rulings by the 5th and 8th circuits, which held that immigrants accused of illegally entering and remaining in the U.S. must be detained while their deportation cases are pending.

The high court agreed to hear the case of Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a citizen of Brazil. Authorities say he entered the United States illegally two decades ago and applied for asylum in 2016. He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory following his September 2025 arrest.

He has never been charged or convicted of a crime, his attorneys said. The court is expected to hear the case in the coming months.

President Donald Trump's administration had urged the high court to take up a different but related case that involves the broader constitutional implications of the new policy.

Attorneys from the Republican administration argue the circuits' split is "disrupting the orderly administration of immigration law." They say the nation's courts have been inundated with thousands of petitions filed by immigrants challenging the government's legal interpretation.

"The result is an unworkable patchwork of inconsistent immigration enforcement, where aliens present without admission are subject to mandatory detention in some circuits but are entitled to bond hearings and often released in others," lawyers for the administration wrote.

The plaintiffs are immigrants represented by the American Civil Liberties Union, which says hundreds of district court judges have joined most circuits in rejecting the Trump administration's new reading of the statutes. Plaintiffs' lawyers say the administration is trying to deny bond hearings for immigrants apprehended anywhere in the U.S. — no matter how long they've lived in the country — rather than limiting the restriction to noncitizens stopped at the border.

"Millions of noncitizens could be affected by the government's new interpretation," ACLU attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration says its new mandatory detention policy is legal under a 1996 immigration law. The policy change departs from the practices of prior administrations, which typically allowed most noncitizens without criminal records to request a bond hearing if they were arrested away from the border.

Follow the AP's coverage of the U.S. Supreme Court at https://apnews.com/hub/us-supreme-court.

title: U.S. passports are getting a new look — and a much easier way to apply
description:
The U.S. government has revealed a new, redesigned passport and announced plans to dramatically modernize the way Americans can apply for one.
Speaking at President Donald Trump’s America.gov Event on September 29, U.
fullText:
The U.S. government has revealed a new, redesigned passport and announced plans to dramatically modernize the way Americans can apply for one.

Speaking at President Donald Trump's America.gov Event on September 29, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio demonstrated a new passport application process that he said U.S. citizens can "complete entirely from home" and showed off a "beautiful" new U.S. passport that’s expected to roll out in 2028.

The changes are part of the Trump administration's new AI-powered government services platform, America.gov, which he launched on Tuesday, touting it as a "single digital point of entry" designed to simplify how Americans access government services.

The last major U.S. passport redesign was introduced in 2021, following the 2016 redesign of the passport book’s overall format and security features. The 2028 update therefore represents another significant modernization within a relatively short period, reflecting continued efforts to strengthen security, incorporate new technologies, and improve document durability and usability.

Perhaps the biggest change that Rubio announced is that first-time passport applicants will no longer need to navigate the traditional, paper-based process.

According to Rubio, Americans will be able to apply for their first passport entirely online beginning next year through America.gov. Applicants will log in through login.gov, use information already held by the government, upload a passport photo from their device, pay online, and track the status of their application digitally; "No printing forms, no drugstore hostage photo, no appointment, no line, no middleman," he said.

The State Department demonstrated the process, showing how users can take their own passport photo at home, preview how it will appear on the passport, submit the application, and then pay for it securely, without filling in any forms or attending in-person appointments.

Rubio added that the platform also provides real-time tracking, so applicants can see exactly when their new passport will arrive.

He said the goal is for the "vast majority of Americans" to be able to apply for a passport or passport card through the online platform by the end of 2027.

Rubio also unveiled what he says is a "uniquely American" design that will become the next generation of the U.S. passport.

Rubio described the redesign as a celebration of American history and identity, centered on the American eagle—the "emblem of American strength and freedom." While the eagle has long appeared on the passport cover, the new version gives it a much more prominent role throughout the document.

The new cover features a larger "more gold" Great Seal, the official national emblem of the U.S. government, and a more prominent display of the words "United States of America," according to Rubio.

Inside, the passport pages show major moments in U.S. history, from the American Revolution and westward expansion to the raising of the flag on Iwo Jima and NASA's Artemis missions, a nod to America's modern space exploration efforts.

Another new visual feature that Rubio also presented was an animation that gives the impression of an eagle in flight when passport holders flip through the pages.

The 2028 "Flight of the Eagle" passport can be viewed alongside earlier commemorative editions such as the 2026 Patriot Passport as part of a broader tradition of using U.S. travel documents to reflect national history and symbolism. Earlier designs likewise combined enhanced security features with imagery intended to express American identity.

For most travelers, the practical benefits are likely to come from the digital application process rather than the passport's appearance.

The online process could reduce the need for in-person appointments, printed paperwork, and third-party passport assistance services that charge fees to help applicants navigate through the application process. Rubio argued that the current system has created opportunities for outside companies to profit from a process that should be more straightforward.

Travelers are also expected to gain access to improved application tracking, including estimated delivery dates and real-time status updates. Rubio noted that Americans have historically had better visibility into tracking their fast food takeaway deliveries than passport processing.

Existing U.S. passports will remain valid until their stated expiration date, provided they remain otherwise valid (for example, not damaged or invalidated). The State Department explicitly says passports issued with older designs can still be used for international travel while valid.

The redesigned passport itself is not expected to change international travel requirements. Instead, the overhaul is intended to update the document's look and presentation while maintaining the high security standards associated with U.S. passports.

Rubio described the passport as one of the world's most trusted identity documents and said the new version would remain highly secure.

Taken together, the changes represent one of the most significant updates to the U.S. passport system in years, combining a fully digital application experience with a redesigned travel document that officials say reflects 250 years of American history.

title: Judge permanently dismisses Reflecting Pool vandalism case against ex-Olympian
description:
— A judge in the nation's capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.
D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn's case with "prejudice," which would block U.S.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — A judge in the nation's capital agreed on Thursday to permanently dismiss a criminal case charging a former Olympian with vandalizing the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a move that could prevent federal prosecutors from reviving the case under political pressure from President Donald Trump.

D.C. Superior Court Judge Todd Edelman ordered the dismissal of David Hearn's case with "prejudice," which would block U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro's office from refiling the felony charge against him. The judge ruled nearly a month after hearing attorneys' arguments.

Hearn's lawyers say Trump administration officials have continued to falsely accuse the Maryland resident of vandalizing the reflecting pool despite Pirro's decision to drop the case on July 31. Trump responded by saying Pirro "choked" and "folded like an umbrella."

Edelman said the case presents "exceptional circumstances" that warrant dismissing the case permanently. He agreed with defense attorneys that the government "shot first and asked questions later" by charging Hearn in a "a lightning-fast indictment process."

"While the government wishes to hold open the possibility of the development of evidence that would support a future prosecution, its own representations make plain that such a possibility is theoretical at best, and more likely, is simply fanciful," the judge wrote.

Permanently dismissing the case protects Hearn from prosecutors electing to revive the case under political pressure from Trump, the judge said.

"Although the prosecutors assigned to this case have deemed it meritless, the President of the United States has repeatedly disparaged them and pressured them to change course," Edelman wrote.

In a court filing in July, Pirro said new evidence produced by the Interior Department showed Hearn wasn't responsible for damage to the pool's lining. Pirro's office attributed the damage instead to a botched installation by a contractor as well as a rush to complete the project in time for this summer's America 250 celebration in Washington.

Pirro's admission was an embarrassing setback for the White House. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum has backed Trump's claims that vandals damaged the pool.

Hearn has said he was on a bike ride on June 19 when he reached in to examine the pool's newly peeled coating and briefly touched a chunk attached to the side of the pool. But he said he obeyed a park worker's command to let go of it.

Hearn was charged with one count of property destruction, which carries a maximum prison sentence of 10 years. His lawyers questioned whether prosecutors properly presented the grand jury with adequate evidence to support the charge and the amount of damage alleged by the government.

Hearn, 67, of Bethesda, Maryland, competed in three Summer Olympics, earning his best finish, ninth, at the 1996 Atlanta Olympic Games, the U.S. Olympic and Paralympic Committee says on its website.

Trump, a Republican, appointed Pirro, a former Fox News host, to serve as the top federal prosecutor for the District of Columbia. Edelman was nominated to the bench by Democratic President Barack Obama.

Hearn's attorneys said the ruling is "a victory for the rule of law and for an innocent American seeking justice" and allows Hearn to "move forward with his life as he deserves."

"This administration chose to pursue an unjust prosecution against Mr. Hearn. It should not get repeated chances to wield the power of criminal prosecution against someone who should never have been prosecuted," the lawyers said in a statement.

fullText:
Trump defended such a move, saying Biden "gave pardons to everyone."

President Donald Trump said in an interview out Thursday that he would be open to pardoning members of his administration, pointing to former President Joe Biden’s blanket pardon to relatives and members of the administration out of concern they would be politically targeted after he left office.

"Yeah, sure, I'd do that," the president answered when asked by TIME magazine earlier this week if he was "considering pardoning members of your administration prior to the end of your term?"

The president further said that Biden "gave pardons to everyone."

Biden issued preemptive pardons to several close family members in the final minutes of his presidency in 2025, saying that his family "has been subjected to unrelenting attacks and threats, motivated solely by a desire to hurt me" and that he had "no reason to believe these attacks will end" after he left office.

Those pardons included James Biden, Joe's younger brother; Sara Jones Biden, James' wife; Valerie Biden Owens, Joe's younger sister; John T. Owens', Valerie's husband; and Francis W. Biden, Joe's younger brother.

In 2024, Biden pardoned his son, Hunter Biden, who was convicted on tax evasion and federal gun charges.

Trump's pardon comments mark the first time he has publicly said he would consider pardoning members of his administration.

Last year, he issued pardons to some to his political and financial supporters as well as several high-profile individuals allegedly involved in his attempt to overturn the election. In his first term, he pardoned several advisers, members of his campaign and one former member of his administration, former National Security Advisor Michael Flynn.

In the interview, Trump expressed his belief that if the Democrats emerge victorious in the midterm elections, “they'll probably go after" him, but he said he will also target them back.

Trump still expressed confidence that Republicans will "do okay" in November, as long as he is on the campaign trail.

"No, I think we'll do okay if I campaign, and I intend to," he said, when asked if he believes that Democrats will take control of Congress.

He then went on to tout some of his endorsement victories including for Republicans Darline Graham and Ed Gallerin -- who defeated Rep. Thomas Massie in the primary for Kentucky’s 4th Congressional District.

Asked about his record low poll numbers, Trump called them "fake" and insisted that he could easily beat anybody who ran against him.

"They're fake numbers. I would beat anybody running today by 20 points," Trump said. "Your numbers that you have are fake."

Trump's cover of TIME magazine will mark his 56th such appearance, according to the outlet. That's more than any other figure in history, surpassing former President Richard Nixon's record.

Trump's interview will be the cover story for TIME's Oct. 26 issue.

fullText:
WASHINGTON, Oct 1 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump said he regretted nominating three Supreme Court justices — Neil Gorsuch, Amy Coney Barrett and ‌Brett Kavanaugh — who have opposed him in recent rulings, according ‌to a Time Magazine interview.

The Republican president was asked about his recent comments regarding the ​three conservative justices in the interview, which was conducted on Monday.

"Do you regret nominating them?" the interviewer asked, referring to Trump's comments in a recent Truth Social post.

"Yeah. Yeah," Trump responded, according to a transcript of the ‌interview.

"What can I do? ⁠I put them in. They voted against me too often. I was very — I gave them the position of ⁠a lifetime, and they vote against me often."

Trump appointed Gorsuch, Kavanaugh and Barrett during his first term as president, building a 6-3 conservative majority and allowing the court ​to steer ​a dramatic rightward course since 2020.

"I ​do like loyalty, yeah," Trump ‌told the interviewer, who then asked whether that was what he wanted from the justices.

"No, I don't want loyalty. I want good decisions," Trump said.

After the top US judicial body declined to allow a Postal Service rule restricting the use of mail-in ballots in the November midterm elections, ‌Trump said his appointees were behaving differently ​than they had during interviews.

"These are not ​the people I interviewed to ​serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are ‌merely a shell of their original ​selves," he wrote on ​Truth Social.

After the court in February struck down his sweeping global tariffs that it found he had imposed illegally using a ​law meant for national ‌emergencies, Trump reserved special ire for Gorsuch and Barrett, who were in ​the majority in that 6-3 ruling.

title: Pentagon used emergency measure to change voter forms for Americans abroad
description:
Democrats filed a lawsuit Thursday over the Trump administration’s recent use of an emergency measure to make changes to the federal voter-registration form used by U.S. service members abroad and citizens residing outside the country, arguing that it’s an attempt to disenfranchise eligible American voters.
The lawsuit follows concerns by advocates for American citizens overseas, who said the changes will spark confusion among eligible voters abroad and officials within U.S.
fullText:
Democrats filed a lawsuit Thursday over the Trump administration's recent use of an emergency measure to make changes to the federal voter-registration form used by U.S. service members abroad and citizens residing outside the country, arguing that it's an attempt to disenfranchise eligible American voters.

The lawsuit follows concerns by advocates for American citizens overseas, who said the changes will spark confusion among eligible voters abroad and officials within U.S. election offices. The Pentagon has saidthe changes are meant to align the form with federal law. More than 2 million Americans living abroad are eligible to cast their ballots in U.S. elections.

The new version of the form changes ID requirements and eliminates a checkbox that allows a voter to declare, "I am a US citizen living outside the country, I have never lived in the United States." That category, sometimes referred to as "never resideds," encompasses the adult children of U.S. citizens who have long lived abroad.

The Democratic National Committee's lawsuit against the Pentagon and the Office of Management and Budget argues that the federal government manufactured an emergency to justify infringing on the voting rights of "never resideds." The DNC is asking the court to declare that the agencies acted unlawfully, stop the federal government from distributing the recently altered version of the form and direct the Pentagon to reissue a previous version of the form.

Doris Speer, president of the Association of Americans Resident Overseas, said she believes the changes to the form, known as the Federal Post Card Application, are "an effort to deter the overseas vote, not to legally stop people from voting but to make the process so difficult that you really have to want to vote to get through it. The result will be confusion, chaos and fewer overseas votes."

The changes to the form follow the Trump administration's unsuccessful efforts to restrict voting by mail and pass sweeping voter ID legislation. That proposed legislation, the Save America Act, would require Americans to prove their citizenship when registering to vote and show photo ID to vote, and permit the Department of Homeland Security to obtain access to voter rolls.

The political stakes of the upcoming midterm election are high for the GOP. Republicans are in danger of losing their majority in the House of Representatives, and Democrats have vowed to step up their investigations into President Donald Trump if they are in the majority.

In August, the Pentagon sought emergency approval to make several changes to the FPCA, used by U.S. voters abroad to register to vote and request an absentee ballot. The Pentagon did not solicit public feedback on the change, as normally would be a part of the process for a document change of this nature.

The Pentagon told The Washington Post in a statement that recent updates were made "to streamline voter identification instructions and ensure alignment with Federal law" but did not detail which federal law. The Pentagon also did not explain what emergency allowed the government to expedite the form changes.

In an Aug. 13 letter to OMB's Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs seeking emergency processing to alter the form, Deputy Undersecretary of War for Personnel and Readiness Sean O'Keefe wrote that the changes were necessary because the previous version of the document may have confused "voters about the information they are required to provide under Federal law and their eligibility to use these forms to register and vote."

In justifying the emergency, O'Keefe wrote that "the next Federal election is fewer than 90 days away, so there is insufficient time to modify" the forms via the standard process, adding that "public harm is reasonably likely to result if normal clearance procedures and time periods are followed."

Elections are typically scheduled years in advance. Tammy Patrick, a longtime elections administrator who serves as the chief program officer at the National Association of Election Officials, and other advocates for U.S. voters overseas say they still don't understand what constituted an emergency in this case.

"I don't think there is an actual emergency," Patrick said. "I have not heard from any election officials about anything related to our infrastructure, neither at the state level … nor at any local level, causing any major concern within our hundreds and hundreds of members."

A 1986 law established federal protections for military and overseas voters. But states determine voter eligibility rules and residence requirements. Currently, "never resideds" are eligible to vote in 37 states based on their parents' previous residence.

Along with changes to the form itself, the General Services Administration's website for the newly altered form also states that it "is for absent Uniform Service members, their families, and citizens residing outside the U.S. intending on returning only." Previously, the federal government made no distinction on who was eligible to use the form based on whether an American citizen intended to return to the United States.

Susan Dzieduszycka-Suinat, president and CEO of the nonprofit U.S. Vote Foundation, said that changing the form "without an effective public comment process sends a terrible message to the people who have always been part of it: election officials, usability experts, and organizations like ours. That process used to give us a form that supported voter participation and made life easier for election administrators."

Speer, with the Association of Americans Resident Overseas, said she wasn't interested in mounting a legal fight ahead of the midterm election, arguing that any effort to stop the federal government from using the new form could create even more confusion for voters. But Dzieduszycka-Suinat said U.S. Vote Foundation is "investigating this issue and the emergency process that was used with legal counsel." She said the organization is prepared to fight in court.

Eligible "never resided" voters must now seek their ballots through states, rather than through the federal government.

California, for example, is one of 37 states that allow a U.S. citizen who never has lived in the United States to vote if their parent or legal guardian was previously registered to vote as a resident of the state. The California secretary of state's office told The Post that the state's online voter-registration application continues to include a category for U.S. citizens who "have never resided in the U.S."

title: FCC chair says government-funded Trump ads ‘don’t raise any red flags’
description:

fullText:
Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr said Wednesday that new pro-Trump TV ads paid for with government funds don’t “merit any sort of FCC review.”

“It doesn’t strike me as anything at all out of the ordinary,” Carr said of the ads, which have aired across the country in recent weeks.

Asked about allegations that the ads are “propaganda,” Carr laughed.

The White House has “explained that these are just normal-course public service announcements, PSAs, that you see all the time. I don’t think there’s anything unique or different about it,” he said at a news conference.

“There’s nothing in there that strikes me that merit any sort of FCC review,” said Carr, whom Trump appointed to the agency.

A reporter pointed out that the progressive advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint with the FCC noting that the Trump campaign used one of the ads in 2024.

Carr brushed off the concern, telling reporters that “there’s groups on the left that have, you know, long worked and pushed to weaponize the FCC’s license renewal process” but that the ads “don’t raise any red flags.”

Public Citizen did not immediately respond to a request for comment Wednesday.

Anna Gomez, the lone Democratic commissioner on the FCC, told NBC News in a statement, “I recognize the concern shared by others that taxpayer dollars are being used to promote a political message, particularly given the timing of these ads coming so close to an election.”

“While it is not surprising to see the FCC exercise a double standard when it comes to its investigative decisions, I am certain we will hear more about this from folks in Congress, who are ultimately responsible,” her statement said.

The use of federal funds to pay for the ads has drawn bipartisan criticism, with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., saying they “shouldn’t be paid for with taxpayer dollars” and Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., calling them an “absolute violation of what democracy is supposed to look like.”

Trump defended the ads when asked about them Wednesday in the Oval Office.

“I’m not running for office and I don’t talk about anybody,” he said. “When I’m talking about making America great, making our country great, that’s a countrywide ad. That’s an ad for the spirit of our country.”

“Now, if somebody said that that’s wrong, I’ll gladly pay the money. But these are ads for the country,” he added.

The first of the ads features Trump describing how he wants to “defeat communism” while the song “Love Me” by JMSN plays in the background.

Another spot is a slightly shorter version of a 2024 Trump campaign ad, which shows him walking down a hallway as he asks people in a voice-over to join him in his “final battle” to “demolish the deep state” and “expel the warmongers from our government.”

In its complaint Tuesday, Public Citizen said that the messages are thinly veiled campaign ads timed to motivate Trump’s supporters ahead of the upcoming midterm elections and that they are unlawful.

“Federal law explicitly prohibits using appropriated public funds for government propaganda, self-aggrandizement, or partisan political advertising. Yet, that is exactly the nature of Trump’s recent campaign ads,” the complaint says, adding that none of the ads to date “meet the standard of a public service announcement.”

“They do not refer to any specific governmental program and they do not serve the purpose of informing the public about any specific governmental program,” the complaint says.

Carr has made headlines for using his post to go after late-night comedians like Stephen Colbert and Jimmy Kimmel and network programs that he has alleged have liberal biases.

The FCC issued an order this year directing Disney’s eight owned-and-operated television stations to file their broadcast license renewals ahead of schedule after the White House and ABC clashed over a joke Kimmel made about first lady Melania Trump.

Disney is challenging the review with a suit alleging the FCC is seeking to coerce and retaliate against “a network that refuses to bow to the ⁠administration’s ​demands.” Carr has said the ABC license review stems from the FCC’s probe of Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion practices — not “speech.”

title: White House removes CNN from press pool for Trump's upcoming trip to Texas and Oklahoma
description: President Donald Trump speaks to the media aboard Air Force One on its way to Joint Base Andrews, Md., from Ireland on Sept. 13.
fullText:
The White House on Wednesday removed CNN from the press pool that’s set to cover a trip by President Donald Trump on Thursday, escalating a feud with the cable network after a federal judge blocked the administration’s push to restrict its media access.

CNN had been designated to travel with Trump on Thursday, according to a press rotation document the White House released Sunday. But when the daily guidance came out for his scheduled visit to a truck manufacturing facility in Denton, Texas, followed by remarks in Durant, Oklahoma, it did not list CNN as providing pool coverage.

The move comes less than a week after a federal judge halted Trump’s effort to ban CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House. It also comes after the White House barred CNN from flying on Air Force One over the weekend when Trump traveled to Tennessee, when the network was scheduled to provide pool coverage. (The judge’s order was limited to media access on the White House grounds.)

Emily Kuhn, a spokesperson for CNN, confirmed the cable network’s removal from planned pool coverage but did not provide additional comment. Instead, she pointed to an earlier statement from Theodore Boutrous, an attorney representing CNN, MS NOW and Politico in their fight with the White House over press access.

“As we have said from the beginning, the President’s ban of CNN, MS NOW and POLITICO from the White House is a blatant violation of the First Amendment and due process,” Boutrous said in a statement Monday, when the three news outlets asked a federal judge to extend his pause on Trump’s ban.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment about CNN’s exclusion from Thursday’s trip.

The White House press pool is a group of media outlets that share video, editorial information and costs for coverage of high-profile officials and events involving the president anywhere in the world. Under the system, each day’s designated “poolers” represent the wider press corps to document newsworthy events and serve as a conduit between the president and the public.

The White House Correspondents’ Association, the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and a group of 49 news and media organizations that included NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, filed a legal brief last week in support of CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

Other member networks of the pool — Fox News, ABC News, CBS News and NBC News — briefly boycotted participating in pool duties last week in solidarity with CNN.

NBC News did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the exclusion of CNN for Thursday’s trip and whether it intended to take any action.

Trump has restricted access for other news outlets before. In 2025, he banned The Associated Press from the Oval Office, Air Force One and certain events for not referring to the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America — his preferred name for the gulf.

The AP sued, and the case continues.

fullText:
Exclusive: Campaign comes amid backlash against tech company’s involvement with Israeli military and Trump’s ICE crackdown

UK politics live – latest updates

Tens of thousands of people have formally demanded NHS England blocks the Palantir-powered national medical data platform from handling their personal information.

More than 44,000 people have filed legal objections to their health data being shared with, stored in or used by the nationwide Federated Data Platform (FDP) operated using the US company’s AI technology.

The coordinated campaign utilises rights enshrined in data protection laws and means the NHS must stop using the data unless it can provide a “compelling reason” to continue.

Hundreds of thousands of people have signed petitions demanding the government cancels its £330m deal with Palantir, and Andy Burnham will be required to make a decision to back or axe Palantir within months.

Campaigners have voiced anger at Palantir’s work for the Israeli military and Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, and two House of Commons select committees have called for Labour to exercise a break clause in the seven-year deal which comes into force in February 2027.

David Murray, a retired IBM systems engineer and one of those requesting the data block, said: “I am a believer in the NHS having really good data on their patients, but I want it to be something you can really trust to be used for the right purposes. I am not happy about Palantir’s involvement with the IDF in Gaza and ICE in America.”

On Wednesday, the human rights group Amnesty International and patient campaign group, Just Treatment, parked a van styled like a shot-up Palestinian ambulance outside Palantir’s London HQ in a stunt that asked: “Why should a company linked to Israel’s destruction of Gaza’s healthcare system have any place in ours?”

Protesters have also raised concerns, acknowledged by the NHS England chief executive, Jim Mackey, that the benefits to public health from the Palantir-powered platform may not be as significant as has been claimed.

Palantir says the FDP, which is designed to connect sprawling health service data on topics ranging from surgery schedules to discharge planning, is helping to cut waiting lists and frees up beds. Louis Mosley, the company’s executive vice-president for UK and Europe, has accused people who disagree with that assessment of suffering from “Palantir derangement syndrome”.

A spokesperson said: “Palantir software is helping to deliver better care, with trusts using it recording 117,000 additional operations, a 14.3% reduction in discharge delays for long-stay patients and a 5.6% improvement in the number of people finding out whether or not they have cancer within 28 days.”

Mosley has said its technology was used for locating hostages, not military targeting, in Gaza, although when challenged last year by a protester alleging “Palantir kills Palestinians” in Gaza, the company’s chief executive, Alex Karp, replied: “Mostly terrorists, that’s true.”

The formal objections to the FDP using personal data cite article 21 of the UK General Data Protection Regulation and express concern that “the involvement of Palantir undermines my personal trust in NHS data confidentiality”. Palantir said its patient data could only be handled according to the NHS’s instructions and remained in the UK.

Veronica Hawking, the campaigns director at 38 Degrees, a not-for-profit that coordinated the data objections, said: “The scale of this public backlash should be a huge wake-up call for the government.”

A spokesperson for NHS England said: “All NHS organisations remain in control of their data within the FDP, with suppliers unable to access it for their own purposes, and we will respond to the objection requests in line with data protection law.”

The 44,000 objectors have also asked that the NHS halts processing of their data through the Palantir platform while their main request is assessed.

fullText:
Democratic governor sharply critical of Donald Trump for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations

Governor Gavin Newsom signed laws Wednesday aimed at protecting California workers from the threats of artificial intelligence , including potential job losses and workplace surveillance.

The laws ban employers from using the technology to predict a worker’s emotional state by using their biometric data, require employers to send written notices to workers if AI is responsible for mass layoffs and ban employers from relying on AI to decide to fire someone.

The Democratic governor also signed an executive order to require state agencies to continue to refer to the technology as “artificial intelligence” instead of the term “super intelligence” as Donald Trump recently ordered US diplomats to use.

“AI should expand opportunity – not come at the expense of workers and families,” Newsom said in a statement. “As this technology reshapes the workplace, California is putting people at the center.”

He sharply criticized Trump at an hour-long event with reporters Wednesday for not passing comprehensive federal AI regulations at a time when industry leaders are warning about the technology’s risks. Trump said Tuesday that top tech leaders signed a voluntary accord to “self-police” AI development.

The governor signed a law this month requiring operators of AI chatbots to perform risk assessments before rolling them out and an executive order requiring the state to consult with experts to further improve oversight over the industry.

“We have to do a lot 

The news conference came on Newsom’s last day to sign or veto bills before he terms out in January. He started the event by signing a law creating a tax credit program aimed at helping local news organizations – including newspapers, digital outlets and TV stations – hire and retain journalists. Newsom criticized what he called Trump’s assault on a free press, pointing to the president’s barring of news organizations from the White House.

Newsom also spoke about the upcoming midterms, which will decide control of Congress. He involved himself early in that fight by leading Democrats last year in a redistricting battle to improve their chances of winning more House seats. He’s said repeatedly that the stakes are high if his party doesn’t succeed in November.

“There will not be a free and fair election in 2028 unless we take back the House of Representatives,” he said Wednesday.

Asked if he had set a deadline for himself to decide to run for president in 2028, Newsom hedged, saying: “That moment will arrive when it arrives.”

Former Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, who, like Newsom, hails from the San Francisco Bay Area, has also said she’s considering running for the job in 2028. Newsom told CNN recently that he would not run for president if she entered the race. He said the two have not spoken since that interview aired.

Newsom weighed in on a proposal to temporarily raise taxes on billionaires that will be on the ballot in November, which he’s consistently opposed. He said he respects supporters of the measure, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders, who are committed to addressing income inequality in the country.

“He’s spot on about the balance between the rich and the poor,” Newsom said. “On this issue, we fundamentally disagree.”

Newsom’s remarks came hours before a gubernatorial debate between Democrat Xavier Becerra and Republican Steve Hilton.

“You’re going to ask me, ‘Are you going to watch the debate?’” he said. “No.”

title: PSA: Trump Continues To Commit Crimes
description: Elie...
fullText:
How the subscription squeeze is ending.

While the president is unlikely to face any consequences for his patently illegal, taxpayer-funded ads, it’s essential to remember he should.

Like many Americans, I was watching college gladiatorial sports on Saturday when a new Donald Trump campaign ad interrupted my nachos and circus. In the ad, Trump promises to rid the country of communists and Marxists—which made me glare at my TV long enough to mumble, “I’m not going anywhere, you piece of shit”—followed by a curious tagline: “Paid for by the U.S. government.”

The line immediately activated my lawyer brain. Federal law prohibits taxpayer dollars from being used for campaign ads and other forms of propaganda. Trump’s ad was a clear violation of this restriction. Moreover, the ad violates the Hatch Act, which bars federal officials from making campaign statements in their official capacity. Nothing about these ads (Trump apparently made three different ones with our tax dollars) is remotely legal, or okay.

And yet, before the game resumed, I knew how the rest of the story would play out. Democrats would demand an “investigation” into this facially obvious violation. Republicans would shrug and either say they hadn’t seen it, or that it was no big deal. The Trump administration would offer some limp legal defense that amounted to “but a Black president existed.” Nothing would happen. All the while, the stories highlighting the ad’s illegality would draw more attention to the state propaganda beamed into our eyeballs.

It’s played out pretty much as I anticipated. Popular ethicists like Richard Painter and Norm Eisen have excoriated the administration. Eisen told The New York Times: “The president and his administration have gone from breaking the law to trampling it.” Senator Elizabeth Warren told The Hill: “There should be a full investigation because on its face it appears to be a violation of federal law.” Even the Republican Senate majority leader John Thune pushed back a little, though he had to be careful to still lick Trump’s boot while lightly admonishing his dear leader. Thune said: “It’s a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars.”

For its part, the Trump administration has called the ad a “public service announcement” and likened it to (wait for it) Barack Obama’s ads encouraging people to The White House said the ad is about “reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”

Friends, there is no “public service” announced in these ads. There is no program or opportunity Trump is offering me. He’s not reminding me to He’s not even telling me to meddle in other people’s business, or spy on my Muslim neighbors like those “if you see something, say something” ads. It’s just a straight campaign ad.

Indeed, we know it’s a campaign ad, because it’s like all of Trump’s other campaign ads. It has all the Trump ticks: he’s alone, walking in a dark hallway to ominous music. Think about it this way: the most famous public service announcement that nearly everyone is familiar with is the “The More You Know” series. Those ads are punctuated with a freaking rainbow and a star. They don’t look like a dystopian murder mystery that is apparently the only page in the Trump style guide.

Trump is using taxpayers dollars for illegal state propaganda, and the penalty for that will be… nothing. You could make the argument that this is an impeachable offense for Trump, but at this point you’d have to be a naive fool to think that the president who has been convicted of 34 felonies will be impeached over this light embezzlement of public funds. If we still had a functional media the outrage over these ads would reach such a level of distraction that Trump would be compelled to pull them and fire a sacrificial staffer for the offense; indeed, it wasn’t too long ago that Trump fired Kristi Noem ostensibly because she misused taxpayer funds for a personal ad campaign. But Noem is a woman, and Trump is Trump, and Trump never takes personal responsibility for his actions. Most likely, he will continue running these ads for a couple of weeks to prove he does not care about laws, then quietly pull them after enough Republicans beg him to do so because it’s not actually helping them in their campaigns to retain power.

And that will be that. Another brazen illegality, another misappropriation of public funds, and another thing Trump will not be held accountable for.

Nothing will happen, but it’s still important to remember that something should happen. We can’t lose the ability to spot a crime when we see it. Speaking out against state propaganda is the best way to resist it. By spotting it and calling it out for what it is, we remain tethered to reality, no matter how hard the state tries to gaslight us. To quote my favorite line in the entire Star Trek canon: “There are four lights.” Not five. And it is important to shout out the right answer, no matter how many times the government tries to lie to you.

It’s also important to remember the truth, because if the Democrats ever take back power, the laws Trump has broken are among those that will need to be fixed and strengthened. The Hatch Act has been violated so many times by the Trump administration it no longer functionally exists. We’re going to need a new one, with real teeth, that will actually deter public officials from campaigning on the taxpayers’ dime. We’re going to need new FCC laws, updated for a digital streaming age, to ensure equal time for candidates while also defanging the institution so it can’t menace Jimmy Kimmell and Stephen Colbert.

We’re going to need to fix a lot of things before we can eat nachos and watch football in peace.

Between the reemergence of right-wing red-baiting and Donald Trump’s use of the chilling National Security Presidential Memorandum–7 to criminalize left political organizing, we’re seeing McCarthyism reborn before our eyes. 

This assault on democracy cannot be ignored or wished away. Resisting it requires bravery in the face of threats and repression, a steadfast commitment to the truth, and the unwavering belief that we can—and will—overcome this darkness.

We must have an independent media that sets the record straight, unearths corruption and abuses of power, and advances a politics of justice and dignity for all if we’re to win this fight.

That’s why I’m writing to you today. This September, The Nation needs to add 100 monthly donors to sustain our progressive journalism. Your contribution makes the next investigative report, the next truth-speaking column, and the next pathbreaking essay all possible. 

I hope you’ll support our work with a recurring donation today. If you donate $10 or more a month, we’ll send you a brand new “Hands Off the Free Press!” sticker to recognise your commitment to our cause. Please, donate today.

Onward,

Katrina vanden Heuvel
Editor and Publisher, The Nation

Late-night hosts weighed in on Trump’s relationship with tech leaders and the White House’s new AI-powered site

On Tuesday night, late-night hosts discussed a Maha summit in Washington DC, the White House’s new AI-powered website and Donald Trump once again falling asleep on live TV.

On NBC, Seth Meyers focused on the president’s ill-phrased announcement of the US murder rate declining. “We have the best, uh, murder,” Trump said.

“What are you talking about, ‘We have the best murder’?” Meyers responded. “It’s a murder rate, not a murder rating.”

On Monday, Trump also took issue with the claim by the US ambassador to China, David Perdue, claim that he offered to sell weapons to China, saying: “I think he was probably talking about Taiwan.”

“So wait, are you saying that we have an ambassador to China who doesn’t know the difference between China and Taiwan?” asked Meyers. “That’s like if Mr Met showed up to the stadium wearing a Yankees jersey.”

Meanwhile, health officials in Florida have issued a local state of emergency after an outbreak of dengue fever. “Man, RFK Jr has only had the job two years and Florida is already turning into an episode of House,” the host laughed.

The White House has also rebuked criticism of taxpayer-funded TV ads. They said “they are public service announcements that are ‘reminding Americans to love their country’”, explained Meyers, before quipping: “The clearest sign of a healthy relationship is if you have to remind someone to love you.”

Trump reportedly told congressional leaders on Friday that he was revoking nearly $1bn in federal funding.

“Oh God, what’s he doing to the reflecting pool now?” joked Meyers. “Is he adding a waterslide?”

Meyers closed his monologue with news that the makers of a smart glasses brand have recalled frames after customers reported them overheating and causing burns.

“Well, I hate to break it to you,” he said, “but no matter what smart glasses you’re wearing, you’re gonna get burned.”

On Jimmy Kimmel Live! the host discussed Trump hosting all the top tech executives at the White House for a lunch on Tuesday. The guest list included Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and the House speaker, Mike Johnson, “who was there to ask if there was any way that AI could turn him into a real boy”.

In a press conference, Trump announced that he was “changing the name” of AI from “artificial intelligence” to “superintelligence” “So far, everybody likes it,” he added.

“Yes,” responded Kimmel drily. “I’m sure the guy whose company’s name is OpenAI is very excited about this development.

“The idea that our guardrails against AI are being erected by an addled 80-year-old man … It’s like asking your grandpa to set up a wifi router in your house. You just wouldn’t do it.”

The host moved on to talk about the new AI-powered government website America.gov.

“A White House official called America.gov ‘a new front door for the federal government’,” said Kimmel. “You know, we need a new front door because Trump demolished the old front door to build his ballroom.”

Kimmel added that Trump is still trying to blame all of America’s struggles on his predecessor, again branding former president Joe Biden “sleepy” in Oval Office remarks this week. Ironically, Trump fell asleep shortly after.

“Only a few minutes after invoking the name ‘sleepy Joe Biden’, nappy Don Trump drifted off to dreamland on live TV,” Kimmel said.

This week also saw the second annual Maha summit in DC in an event attended by JD Vance, Robert F Kennedy Jr and Mike Tyson.

“You know we’re screwed when the sanest person in the group has half a face tattoo,” Kimmel said.

fullText:
Donald Trump and six tech executives voluntarily signed the document, which included a misspelling, committing to safely developing AI

The White House misspelled “United States” under the signature of Donald Trump on an accord he signed with AI executives on Tuesday.

At the bottom of the accord on “Super Intelligence”, the term Trump has used to rebrand artificial intelligence, the president’s signature appeared as “President of the Unites States”.

It is unclear how the misspelling occurred or whether it will appear in the Federal Register, the database that contains official presidential actions and other government documents.

Trump and six tech executives signed the document voluntarily committing to safely developing AI to address widespread concerns, sparked by industry leaders who warned the technology is evolving too rapidly to control.

Trump has largely brushed aside concerns about AI harming humans and called for companies to continue developing the technology so the US can become the global leader in AI. Even while signing the accord on safety, the US president praised the business executives for growth.

Trump posted the document containing the misspelling on Truth Social, and the White House Communications Team emailed it out shortly after it was signed.

The Bloomberg News correspondent David Gura appeared to be the first to notice the spelling error.

The Guardian has asked the White House for comment

The accord on artificial intelligence outlined four layers of “controls and audits” that companies will implement to ensure AI capabilities operate as intended. That includes “robust” internal controls and partnering with an “independent external auditor or evaluator”.

Potential internal controls could include empowering a team to monitor and detect that AI is operating correctly and creating monitors to ensure AI technologies will not hack or access technical systems in cybersecurity, biosecurity and chemical threats.

External monitors would also check to make sure the AI is operating as intended and companies could designate a committee of the board of directors to oversee reports from teams operating the controls of the AI.

The accord is the first step in addressing concerns, raised by industry experts in mid-September.

Americans have become increasingly skeptical of AI. A recent New York Times/Siena College poll found that 61% of voters opposed the construction of datacenters, while an SSRS/CNN poll found that 71% of Americans believed the government wasn’t doing enough to regulate the growth and development of AI.

While Tuesday’s document is only an accord, it left open the possibility of codifying the framework into formal regulations or laws – something Trump has repeatedly rejected.

“I think I’m seeing tremendous self-policing,” Trump told reporters outside the White House on Tuesday. “And they understand that they have to self-police.”

The six executives who signed the accord are Dario Amodei from Anthropic; Elon Musk from SpaceXAI; Greg Brockman from OpenAI; Jensen Huang from Nvidia; Mark Zuckerberg from Meta; and Sundar Pichai from Google.

title: Trump's tariffs are back in court — again
description: Containers are seen at the container terminal of Nanjing Port, in China's eastern Jiangsu province on September 8, 2026. Most Chinese goods shipped to the United States have faced a minimum 12.5% tax. - AFP/Getty...
fullText:
Here we go again: President Donald Trump's sweeping global tariffs are back under the legal microscope.

On Wednesday, a three-judge panel at the US Court of International Trade is set to hear arguments in a case that could determine whether the president can use a 1970s trade law to impose tariffs on nearly everything the United States imports.

Since late July, goods from 80 countries, including China, India and Japan, have faced tariff rates ranging from 10% to 12.5%. The administration imposed the duties after determining that those countries had allegedly failed to address the use of forced labor in producing goods shipped to the US. The US Trade Representative recommended the tariffs as a remedy, with higher rates applying to countries deemed the "worst offenders."

The rollout of these tariffs coincided with the lapse of a separate 10% near-blanket duty Trump had imposed earlier in the year under a different legal authority. The Supreme Court later ruled that Trump had overstepped his authority, which immediately invalidated the tariffs and triggered $168 billion worth of refunds for importers.

The complaint, filed by the Liberty Justice Center, a libertarian public-interest law firm that successfully won the landmark Supreme Court tariff case, argues that the administration is moving to preserve a predetermined global tariff policy. That, they argue, is an improper use of the trade law commonly referred to as Section 301.

Administration officials, meanwhile, told reporters previously that the timing was to "avoid complexity" that would come from layering the new levies on top of the then-10% duties.

"The real message here that everyone needs to take away is the president is going to always use the tools at his disposal to achieve his trade policy objectives," administration officials said on a briefing call with reporters shortly before the 10%-15% duties took effect.

While Wednesday's arguments may offer clues about how the judges view the case, a ruling could still take weeks — if not months. Either side could then appeal the decision to the US Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, which could also decide whether to pause enforcement of the tariffs while the case proceeds.

The fight could eventually reach the Supreme Court, extending the legal battle for several months more.

title: GOP Sen. Mike Lee blocks effort to bar Trump from demolishing Kennedy Center
description:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president.
fullText:
A Republican senator squashed a bipartisan push to prohibit the Trump administration from demolishing the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.

Sen. Jeff Merkley, D-Oregon, and Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, who lead the Senate panel that oversees funding for the Kennedy Center, tried to pass a bill that would require an act of Congress to demolish any national memorials that honor a president. An objection from a single senator can block a bill from being passed by unanimous consent.

Sen. Mike Lee, R-Utah, objected.

The bill – dubbed the "Protecting Presidential Memorials Act" – would also apply to Lincoln Memorial and Washington Monument. But Merkley and Murkowski made their immediate goal clear.

"This has of course to do with the president planning to demolish the Kennedy Center," Merkley said on the Senate floor late Monday evening, Sept. 28, after the passing of the Protect College Sports Act, a major overhaul to college athletics related to NIL (name, image and likeliness) payment for student athletes.

Lee's office said in a statement to USA TODAY that this effort should go through "the appropriate committee process."

"Democrats should join us in lowering the cost of living and securing American elections instead of wasting the Senate’s time with partisan scaremongering," Lee said in the statement shared by communications director Billy Gribbin.

The Senate vote is the latest chapter in a year of legal wrangling and congressional wrangling over the Kennedy Center.

The Kennedy Center added Trump's name to the building's facade in December 2025 after the board – which was handpicked by Trump – voted to rename the center. In June 2026, a judge ordered that his name be taken down, saying that an act of Congress was needed to change the name of the memorial to the assassinated president.

Trump's name has since been removed, but a tarp remains covering the building's name where Trump's name used to be.

Earlier in September, the Kennedy Center closed after part of the ceiling collapsed, and on Sept. 15 the center's board voted to close the center for two years.

That came after a federal judge's second ruling that Trump's name could not be added to the building in September 2026, the culmination of months of legal disputes as the president contended that the center needed to be renovated, that only he could raise the money for it and that his administration should be recognized for it.

Trump has continued to defend his stance about his name being on the building, saying on Sept. 18 that the center had "been a dump" and "lost money" for years. He said that he would subsidize the necessary repairs but said that his administration should be recognized.

Merkley accused the president of wanting to demolish the center, pointing to an image captured of Trump inside Air Force One reading a poster that appears to say "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." The photo was taken hours after Trump told reporters that the memorial will "end up being ripped down" unless major renovations are undertaken.

title: The US Government Just Launched an AI Chatbot
description: The Trump administration just launched a chatbot for government-related questions.
fullText:
AI is virtually everywhere in 2026; that now includes U.S. government websites. On Tuesday, the Trump administration launched "America.gov," a new website that uses AI to answer questions about the government. While the experience currently feels like ChatGPT running U.S. government-themed instructions, the plan is for America.gov to eventually let you take action as well.

America.gov "combines" the nearly 30,000 websites under the umbrella of the U.S. government into one set of sources. Rather than invite you to browse those tens of thousands of pages to answer your questions, that dataset serves as the basis for the site's proprietary chatbot. You ask the chatbot a question about the U.S. government, and the AI sifts through those websites to generate an answer. It's like ChatGPT, but if the model only had access to U.S. government websites and sources.

You could ask the site how to replace your Social Security card, renew your passport, or register to vote in your state. You could ask for information on changing your address with the USPS, when Medicare open enrollment dates are, or upload a PDF of a government form for assistance. The site says any personal information will be automatically removed, though the privacy policy clarifies that it "will make a best-effort attempt in your browser to remove any private details using Rampart (an open-source classifier system to detect some types of PII, such as Social Security Numbers, phone numbers, email addresses, and credit card numbers)."

The website currently supports three languages—English, Spanish, and French—as well as voice commands, if you prefer speaking to your chatbots rather than typing to them. You don't need an account to use it, nor is there a fee or subscription, and there are no ads.

In its current form, America.gov is a simple chatbot. But the site has bold claims for future features. Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced plans to let users apply for and renew their passports directly through the site, including a dynamic progress tracker to keep tabs on your documents. Other future abilities could include enrolling in Medicare or finding a job with the federal government.

But as with all claims, take these with a grain of salt. The government says these features are coming in early 2027, but this is a tall order for such a project. A single website that lets you complete complex government processes with the simplicity of a chatbot sounds great, but it would need to be accurate and reliable for all possible tasks and functions. It would certainly take significant proof of security and dependability for me to trust such a program with renewing my passport or helping me enroll in health care.

It's impossible to discuss America.gov without acknowledging the administration that is spearheading the project. One would assume that an AI-powered government website developed by this administration would be biased towards Trump and his many falsehoods. And yet, the tool is astoundingly neutral, to the point where I can only imagine how frustrated Trump would be by some of these answers.

The first question many tested America.gov with was "Who won the 2020 election?" Donald Trump famously and frequently says that the election was stolen from him, but his new website plainly states that Joseph R. Biden Jr. won. The bot does sometimes tie the answer to the electoral count, stating that Biden won 306 votes to Trump's 232, but I was surprised to see "Joseph R. Biden Jr. won the 2020 presidential election under the official Electoral College count" as an answer on this site.

The site will also tell you that Donald Trump was president when diesel prices hit their highest historic price ($6.529 per gallon as of Sept. 21, 2026.), and that prices are high, in part, due to "military action" affecting the Staight of Hormuz. It will also say that grocery prices were higher in August than they were a year ago, which contradicts Trump's claims that prices have come down under his term.

Of course, Trump-influenced information that appears on official government sites will appear here. Ask it what the body of water that abuts Texas is called, and it will say the Gulf of America, formerly the Gulf of Mexico. Ask it what lake borders Toronto, Canada, and the bot will say Lake America, formerly Lake Ontario. In both cases, it will refer to the executive orders that changed those names.

Typically, I'd be worried about an AI tool hallucinating its answers and providing incorrect information to users. That's still a concern here, of course. But by creating a chatbot that only pulls information from official government sources, Trump has inadvertently created an official government fact-checker. And unless Trump starts injecting these sites with the same falsehoods he tells in interviews and on Truth Social, America.gov may be a reasonably reliable source of information.

fullText:
An ancient ground carving that was severely damaged by the administration’s border wall construction was created before Stonehenge and Egypt’s oldest pyramid, according to recently publicized research.

The Las Playas Intaglio, a giant fish carved into the Sonoran Desert in Arizona, is now considered the oldest example in the Americas of a geoglyphic, the ancient art form that is carved into or drawn on the ground.

In April, contractors hired by the Trump administration to make way for a second wall along the Arizona-Mexico border “scraped” a 50-foot swath through the ancient carving, according to the Center for Biological Diversity, which documented the damage.

The intaglio on the ground of the ancestral homeland of the Tohono O’odham and other Indigenous tribes is estimated to be about 2,000 years older than Egypt’s first pyramid and to have been created about 1,500 years before the first construction of Stonehenge and 4,000 years before Peru’s Nazca Lines, researchers have found.

The formerly 272-foot carving had originally been thought to be about 1,000 years old. But the latest research dates the art’s creation to at least 6,500 years ago, and possibly as much as 7,500 years ago.

That age emphasizes “the significance of this site and the parallel great misfortune resulting from its damage,” the researchers said in an article published in The SAA Archaeological Record.

“This discovery makes an already devastating loss even more profound. It’s a cultural and historical atrocity,” Russ McSpadden, Southwest conservation advocate at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement.

A Customs and Border Protection spokesperson said in an email to NBC News that the contractor “inadvertently disturbed” the site and that CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott has been “engaged directly with tribal leadership to determine appropriate next steps.”

“The remaining portion of the site has been secured and will be protected in place. CBP is conducting a thorough review of construction protocols and strengthening communication procedures to ensure this does not happen again,” the spokesperson stated, adding that the agency is “committed to respecting and safeguarding cultural heritage throughout all border infrastructure projects.”

The damage to that site and construction on other parts of Tohono O’odham land and sacred Indigenous areas has strained the tenuous relationship between the tribal nation and the government. The tribe is appealing a federal judge’s decision refusing to block the administration’s border wall construction through its reservation.

While the intaglio’s site is irreparably damaged, the Tohono O’odham people are trying to stop the government from plowing through Quitobaquito Springs, a desert water source in Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument that is also considered a sacred site and holds endangered species.

In order to build the border wall and barriers, the Department of Homeland Security invoked authority granted in the Secure Fence Act of 2006 to waive numerous laws protecting the environment, water, cultural, historical and religious sites.

The Tohono O’odham Nation has long worked with CBP, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security, on border security, helping to keep drug traffickers and others from using its land for criminal activity.

The tribe’s reservation straddles the U.S.-Mexico border, and its members have permission to move between the two countries with ID checks. About 3,000 of its members are in Mexico, according to the tribal nation.

The Center for Biological Diversity stated in a news release that conservation advocates and tribal nations have long warned that border wall and secondary border barrier plans could cut through sensitive habitat and cultural sites across the region.

Wall construction in other parts of the border has sparked other lawsuits and opposition from landowners, Native American tribes, local governments, conservation groups, business owners and others.

In Texas, a tribal nonprofit for the Lipan Apache and an outdoor recreation business have opposed the border wall construction, alleging DHS is not authorized to violate the Religious Freedom Restoration Act, which they say it would do by destroying or cutting off access to sacred sites.

A federal judge ordered a temporary halt to construction in Big Bend National Park in response to the lawsuit, but construction continues on other parts of the rugged, undeveloped and remote region outside state and federal parkland.

fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Department of Homeland Security has tapped $20 million to pay for the campaign-style ads glorifying President Donald Trump that have drawn widespread criticism from Republicans and Democrats as a blatant misuse of taxpayer dollars that likely runs afoul of anti-propaganda law.

In a letter Tuesday to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, two top Democratic senators said that the money is being drawn from Trump's so-called "One Big Beautiful Bill" and was supposed to go for U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

"We should not have to remind you that using government funding to create or air political ads like the ones that have been running over the last few days is illegal and a shockingly corrupt misuse of taxpayer dollars," wrote Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, and Sen. Chris Murphy of Connecticut, the ranking Democrat on the subcommittee that handles Homeland Security funding.

The senators demanded answers within the next 48 hours about "how this president is literally stealing their tax dollars to air campaign ads celebrating himself."

They asked the secretary if the department plans to use additional federal funds to air these ads or create new ones, and if so to share contracting information with Congress. They also asked Mullin if he had spoken to Trump about using the taxpayer funds for the ads.

The political uproar over Trump's hagiographic ads, which started running last week during popular TV shows, including college and National Football League programming, has not abated as critics on the left and right raise alarms about the use of taxpayer funds, particularly so close to the midterm elections.

The White House has defended the advertisements, which disclose that they are funded by the U.S. government, as public service announcements.

Asked for a request for comment Tuesday on the senators' letter, Homeland Security referred to the earlier White House response.

The unusual commercials, which echo the GOP's midterm election slogans, against imagery of Trump's tenure in office — one with a "Love me, Love me" song refrain in the background — appear to violate a law against congressionally appropriated funds being used for propaganda.

Experts also have said the ads, which are airing on network and cable TV and streaming, differ from other administrations' PSAs because they aren't designed to help Americans access any specific program.

Over the weekend, a new ad promoting the president resembles a black-and-white video from his own 2024 campaign that shows Trump walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a "final battle" against "globalists" and "warmongers." It ends with Trump staring straight into the camera lens with the "Paid for by the U.S. Government" message printed.

Sen. Thom Tillis, a Republican from North Carolina, has compared Trump's ads to those used by authoritarian former leader Viktor Orban of Hungary. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican from South Dakota, said it "shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars."

Data from the outside firm AdImpact shows more than $2.5 million was spent on the three ads over the past seven days. The actual amount spent could be significantly more, depending on whether networks classified the ads as political.

The senators said in their letter that DHS has committed $20 million to the campaign.

A person who was not authorized to discuss the situation and who was granted anonymity confirmed the findings, which were first reported by the Wall Street Journal.

The unusual ad campaign comes as Republicans face an increasingly volatile midterm election season with their control of the House and Senate — and Trump's future agenda — all at risk.

Voters say they are struggling with high prices of gas and groceries, and are concerned about the lengthy U.S. war against Iran, now in its seventh month. Democrats are gearing up for vast oversight of Trump and his administration if they seize power, and impeachment is not off the table.

House Democrats said Trump's director of the Office of Management and Budget, Russ Vought, moved $20 million from Homeland Security resources to the ad campaign on Sept. 19.

The next day, a $20 million contract for a "National Media Campaign" was awarded to the Maryland-based LMD Agency, Inc., according to federal data. LMD Agency did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The Homeland Security funds are part of a whopping $175 billion Congress gave the department in the "Big, Beautiful, Bill" as part of Trump's immigration enforcement and deportation agenda. Democrats voted against that package, which Trump signed into law last summer, in part because of its steep cuts to Medicaid and the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP.

Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, and Rep. Henry Cuellar of Texas, the ranking Democrat on the Homeland Security subcommittee, said that after gutting $1 trillion from Medicaid and social services and "more than quadrupling funding for mass deportations, it turns out the Trump administration used Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill to pay for President Trump's political ads."

They said if the Democrats regain control, they "will work to uncover and reverse misuses of taxpayer money like this and hold those who abused their power accountable."

What's also striking about the administration's use of taxpayer dollars for the ads is that Trump's own political campaign committee, MAGA Inc., is sitting on hundreds of millions of dollars of funding that could be used during the midterm season. Groups aligned with MAGA Inc. have started shelling out funds for the House and Senate races.

The administration has defended the use of taxpayer dollars for the ads and shown no signs of changing course.
